bugs.title: Realtime fan-out silently drops up to 63% of durable messages sent within ~250ms of each other
bugs.frequency: Always (2/2 independent runs, identical numbers)
bugs.preconditions: Two provisioned accounts A and B in one DM. Both hold an open WebSocket and have been greeted with `connected`.
steps: Provision accounts A and B; create their DM.
Open a WebSocket for each with a valid access token; wait for the `connected` frame.
A sends 8 messages via POST /chat/messages back-to-back with no delay. Every send returns 201 with a distinct, monotonically increasing seq.
Wait 5s for fan-out to settle.
Count the durable `message` frames B's socket received.
Repeat with 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1000ms and 1500ms spacing between sends.
bugs.expected: All 8 messages arrive as durable `message` frames at B, at every spacing. The contract is explicit: 'Durable never dropped; ephemeral (typing/presence/receipt/caption) coalesced under backpressure' (docs/backend-integration-reference.md §4), and SendQueue's own docstring says 'durable frames (messages) are NEVER dropped' (libs/feature-realtime/src/fabric/send-queue.ts:10-13).
bugs.actual: Measured loss rate by spacing — 0ms: 3/8 delivered (63% lost); 100ms: 4/8 (50% lost); 250ms: 8/8 (0%); 500ms: 8/8; 1000ms: 8/8; 1500ms: 8/8. Every lost message WAS persisted (all 8 seqs are present in GET /chat/conversations/:id/messages?afterSeq=0), so this is purely a realtime delivery loss, not data loss.
bugs.user_impact: In a live open chat the recipient sees nothing for the majority of a rapid message burst. The sender's ticks never advance past one grey tick for those messages. The mobile client's cursor/afterSeq backfill only recovers them on a reconnect or a detected seq gap, so a user who stays in the foreground can sit in front of a chat that is visibly missing messages.
bugs.suspected_cause: The loss threshold sits at a clean ~250ms boundary, which points at a windowed read in the event-bus consumer between the durable publish and ws-fabric's write path: events arriving inside one window appear to overwrite rather than queue. The per-connection SendQueue was ruled OUT by reading it — durable frames are always pushed (send-queue.ts:22-31) and ws-fabric drains immediately on write (ws-fabric.ts:339-342), so nothing there can drop a durable frame.
bugs.notes: This one defect is the common cause behind VC-002, VC-003 and VC-004 — fix it first and re-test those before triaging them separately.

bugs.title: Blue tick never arrives: a `read` receipt sent in the same tick as `delivered` is lost
bugs.frequency: Always when the two frames are sent without an intervening await (3/3 rounds)
bugs.preconditions: A and B in a DM, both sockets open. A has sent a message acked with seq N.
steps: A sends a message; note the acked seq N.
B writes {kind:'durable',type:'delivered',data:{conversationId,seq:N}} and {kind:'durable',type:'read',data:{conversationId,seq:N}} to its socket with no delay between them.
Wait 5s and list every `receipt` frame A received for seq N.
bugs.expected: A receives both receipts, or at minimum the `read` one (read supersedes delivered), so the sender's tick turns blue.
bugs.actual: A receives only the `delivered` receipt — consistently the FIRST of the two. The `read` receipt never arrives, so the sender stays on a grey double tick indefinitely. Sending the same two frames 1.5s apart delivers both (verified: `delivered@2, read@2`).
bugs.user_impact: Blue ticks are effectively broken for the normal case. The mobile client marks a conversation read on open, which is exactly the same-tick pattern.
bugs.suspected_cause: Same windowing behaviour as VC-001, applied to receipt events. Note the surviving frame is the FIRST, not the latest — so it is not the documented ephemeral coalesce-to-latest in SendQueue (send-queue.ts:22-27), which would have kept `read`.
bugs.rootCause: Unknown — requires engineering investigation. Likely the same defect as VC-001.
bugs.notes: The client-side shape that triggers it: SyncEngine applies delivered then read for the same conversation with no gap.

bugs.title: Read watermark can regress: the higher receipt is lost and a lower one survives
bugs.frequency: Observed 1/1 in the out-of-order test
bugs.preconditions: A has sent 3 messages to B (seqs 24, 25, 26). Both sockets open.
steps: B sends a read receipt at the TOP seq (26).
Wait 2s.
B sends a read receipt at a LOWER seq (24).
Wait 3s and record every read watermark A received.
bugs.expected: The highest watermark A ever observes is 26. A read watermark must be monotonic — a blue tick must never turn back to grey.
bugs.actual: A received only [24]. The receipt for 26 was lost and the later, lower one survived, so A's highest observed watermark is 24 — lower than what B actually reported.
bugs.user_impact: Read state can move backwards on the sender's screen, or stall below the true watermark.
bugs.suspected_cause: Receipt loss (VC-001/VC-002) combined with the absence of a server-side monotonic floor on the fanned-out watermark. Note the CLIENT does enforce monotonicity in its query predicate, but non-atomically (see VC-021), so it cannot fully compensate.

bugs.title: POST /auth/register accepts an arbitrary non-phone string and provisions a full account with real tokens
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: None. /auth/register is @Public.
steps: POST /auth/register {phone:'not-a-phone', platform:'android', devicePubkeyBase64:<valid SPKI base64>}
POST /auth/revotp/webhook with cli:'not-a-phone' and an otherwise-valid missed-call proof
POST /auth/session {sessionId}
bugs.expected: Step 1 is rejected with a 4xx validation error. The phone number is the account's identity anchor — contact discovery and the OPRF blinding key are derived from it — so a non-phone string must never become an account.
bugs.actual: Step 1 returns 201. The webhook returns 200 {verified:true}. /auth/session returns 201 with a real accountId, deviceId, RS256 access JWT and opaque refresh token. A fully usable account exists whose phone is the literal string 'not-a-phone'.
bugs.user_impact: Unbounded junk-account creation, and an identity anchor that contact discovery cannot reason about. Any downstream code that assumes `phone` is E.164 now has a row that violates that.
bugs.suspected_cause: No phone validation on the register DTO. Note /auth/otp/send DOES validate (requireValidPhone in otp.service.ts), so the two entry points disagree.
bugs.rootCause: Unknown — requires engineering investigation (observed: no validation on this path; the OTP path validates).

bugs.title: POST /auth/register accepts a non-base64 device public key, permanently breaking device-key login for that install
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: None.
steps: POST /auth/register {phone:<valid>, platform:'android', devicePubkeyBase64:'!!!not-base64!!!'}
Complete the Reverse-OTP proof.
POST /auth/session.
bugs.expected: Step 1 fails fast with a 4xx. The code comment at auth.service.ts:199 states exactly this intent: 'Fail-fast if the provided key is not valid base64. This prevents a 500 error later in the webhook.'
bugs.actual: All three steps succeed (201 / 200 / 201) and a real token set is issued. The account's device row now holds an unusable public key.
bugs.user_impact: The app's silent re-login path (apps/mobile/src/features/auth/hooks/useAuth.ts:286-291) calls /auth/challenge + /auth/login/device-key on cold start. For an install provisioned this way that can never verify, so the user is dropped to the sign-in screen on every cold start with no explanation.
bugs.suspected_cause: The guard the comment describes is either absent or not reached on this path.

bugs.title: POST /auth/revotp/webhook is @Public with no shared secret — an unauthenticated account-provisioning primitive
bugs.environment: local backend axis6; the same code is deployed to the dev Render environment
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: Network reach to the host. NO credentials of any kind.
steps: POST /auth/register for any phone number (the endpoint is @Public) -> {sessionId}
POST /auth/revotp/webhook with a self-asserted proof: {sessionId, cli:<same phone>, path:'missed-call', originationClass:'mobile', attestation:'genuine', riskScore:1, ts:Date.now()}
POST /auth/session {sessionId} -> a real token set for that phone number.
bugs.expected: The webhook must prove it came from the SIP gateway — a shared secret, a signature (the codebase already has `x-velchat-signature` for inter-service calls), or a network policy that makes the route unreachable from outside.
bugs.actual: The route is declared @Public (auth.controller.ts:31-36) and performs no origin check whatsoever. Every anti-spoof field it validates is supplied by the caller, so a caller simply asserts `originationClass:'mobile'`, `attestation:'genuine'`, `riskScore:1` and passes all five rules. Anyone who can reach the host mints tokens for an arbitrary phone number.
bugs.user_impact: Account takeover of any phone number that has not yet registered, and account creation at will. On a deployment reachable from the internet this is a complete authentication bypass.
bugs.suspected_cause: Acknowledged as incomplete in the code itself: 'Server-to-server only — in prod this edge is locked down by NetworkPolicy + a shared secret (platform task)' (auth.controller.ts:29-30). The platform task has not landed, and nothing fails closed in the meantime.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by code reading: the route has no authentication and no origin verification; the anti-spoof rules validate only caller-supplied fields.
bugs.notes: DISCLOSURE: the QA harness uses this endpoint to provision its test identities, because it is currently the only way to obtain two real sessions without spending SMS. QA/lib/provision.js refuses to run against any non-local host unless QA_ALLOW_REMOTE_PROVISION=true. When this defect is fixed, switch the harness to OTP dev-mode (OTP_DEV_MODE=true) as documented in RUNBOOK.md.

bugs.title: Edge gateway 502s every proxied route while all upstream services are healthy (dev Render deployment)
bugs.frequency: Always (throughout the test session)
bugs.preconditions: All five axis6 services awake and returning 200 on /health at their own origins.
steps: GET https://velchat-{identity,messaging,realtime,content,platform}-service-2aje.onrender.com/health -> 200 for all five.
GET https://velchat-edge-gateway-2aje.onrender.com/health -> 200.
GET https://velchat-edge-gateway-2aje.onrender.com/.well-known/jwks.json -> 502.
Repeat for /auth/otp/send, /users/me, /presence/subscribe, /chat/messages, /notifications/prefs, /search, /media/usage -> 502 on every one.
bugs.expected: The gateway proxies each path to its upstream and returns the upstream's response.
bugs.actual: The gateway's own /health and /ready return 200, but every proxied route returns 502 {error:{code:'BAD_GATEWAY'}} — including routes the upstream serves correctly when called directly (identity-service returns 200 for /.well-known/jwks.json and 401 for /auth/devices at its own origin).
bugs.user_impact: The mobile dev build points API_BASE_URL at this gateway (apps/mobile/.env.dev), so every API call fails. The dev app is completely unusable against the dev backend. This blocked all remote API testing and forced the suite onto a locally-started backend.
bugs.suspected_cause: Upstream host resolution in the gateway (the render.yaml wires upstream hosts via `fromService` host properties). Not investigated further — this is a deployment concern, not a code defect observable from the client.
bugs.notes: Related client-side observation: warmBackend() (apps/mobile/src/infra/network/client.ts:33-62) pings the gateway, the gateway-proxied JWKS route and the realtime host. Because the gateway does not wake or reach its upstreams, that warm-up cannot actually warm identity/messaging/content/platform on Render. See VC-008.

bugs.title: warmBackend() cannot warm the services it targets on the Render topology
bugs.frequency: Always on the Render topology
bugs.preconditions: Render free-tier services hibernated after ~15 min idle.
steps: Cold-start the app so warmBackend() fires.
It requests <gateway>/health, <gateway>/.well-known/jwks.json and <realtime>/health.
Observe which upstreams actually wake.
bugs.expected: The login path (identity-service) is warm by the time the user taps 'Send code', which is the stated purpose of the function.
bugs.actual: Render wakes a service when a request reaches that service's OWN hostname. Only the gateway and the realtime host are addressed directly; identity/messaging/content/platform are only reached via the gateway, which returns 502 without waking them (VC-007). Measured: the gateway woke in 36s and realtime in 43s, while the four other services stayed asleep until each was hit at its own origin.
bugs.user_impact: The first real request after an idle period still eats a 30-50s cold start, which the 60s axios timeout barely covers — the exact failure warmBackend() was written to prevent.
bugs.suspected_cause: The warm-up list is built from the single gateway origin, which does not match the dev deployment's per-service Render topology.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by measurement: gateway-proxied requests do not wake upstream Render services.
bugs.notes:
INVESTIGATED — BLOCKED on information the client does not have. warmBackend() can only ping hosts it knows, and the only per-service origins in config are API_BASE_URL (velchat-edge-gateway-2aje.onrender.com) and WS_URL (velchat-realtime-service-2aje.onrender.com). identity/messaging/content/platform have no hostname anywhere in the repo, so there is nothing to warm them WITH. They appear to share a Render instance suffix (-2aje), which makes a pattern like velchat-identity-service-2aje.onrender.com plausible — but deliberately NOT guessed and baked into a shipping app: a wrong host is at best a wasted request on every cold start and at worst traffic aimed at somebody elses service. To fix, add the real per-service origins to .env.dev/.env.prod (e.g. WARM_ORIGINS as a comma-separated list) and have warmBackend fan its health pings across them; the function already fires them fire-and-forget off the render path, so only the list is missing. Needs the actual Render hostnames from the owner.

FIXED, and the entry itself turned out to be incomplete. THE TOPOLOGY CONTRADICTION IS RESOLVED and .env.prod is right: RUNBOOK 0b (which both env files cite by name) says production is topology mono — every feature group in ONE process behind one URL on the Azure VM — while dev is axis6, six Render services that sleep after ~15 min. backend-integration-reference 3/8 is STALE: it is dated 2026-07-11 and flags the prod origin as unconfirmed at the time, which it no longer is. env.ts already carried the same statement in-repo.

CONSEQUENCE: this entry proposed fanning out to per-service hosts, and that fix is now WRONG — a production build has nothing per-service to warm, ever. The fan-out was only ever a dev concern.

TWO DEFECTS THE ENTRY DID NOT RECORD, both found while verifying: (1) the /.well-known/jwks.json ping was commented auth-service (login path) but is gateway-proxied, so it 502s on dev without identity ever being reached and warmed nothing the /health ping one line above had not — that label is exactly what made the function read to a reviewer as if the login path were covered; (2) in a PRODUCTION build the old code fired THREE requests at an always-awake host, because prod REST and WS share one origin so the ws-derived URL collapses onto the same string. Every prod cold start paid for three pings that could not wake anything. The pre-fix test captured that verbatim.

FIX: a pure warmTargets(env) decision with two invariants — a wake request goes only to a host that actually SLEEPS (Render), and only to an origin appEnv already names, which is the same set the certificate-pinning config is kept in step with. It reuses endpointHost from transportSecurity rather than a second parser so the warm-up and the pinning policy can never disagree about which host a URL names, and it takes a structural {apiBaseUrl, wsUrl} rather than AppEnv so it CANNOT read appEnv.name — VC-035 proved the name can lie while the URL is true. Each surviving ping got an AbortController and a 10s deadline; the old ones were unbounded fetches with no owner on the launch path (M20.3), and RN OkHttp ships with no default read timeout. Net: production and the local dev loop now send ZERO warm requests; the dev Render flavor sends two bounded ones to hosts it was already configured against.

STILL BLOCKED, and no longer on hostnames: warming the other four dev services needs (a) the backend owner to provide a stable alias per service, because RUNBOOK 0b says the Render -2aje suffix must never be copied into config — a service recreated under a new suffix would aim five launch requests at whoever holds those names next; and (b) a domain-config per extra host in the Android network-security config in the same commit, or those hosts ship SILENTLY UNPINNED. It is also not worth unblocking while VC-007 is open, since the dev deployment 502s on every proxied route anyway, and a VC-007 fix may wake the upstreams itself and make the fan-out moot.

SECONDARY, for whoever owns the backend docs: RUNBOOK 0b lists the dev WebSocket as wss://velchat-edge-gateway-2aje.onrender.com/ws, but .env.dev says the edge gateway has no /ws route and no upgrade handler. One of the two is wrong.

bugs.title: POST /conversations/dm returns 404 through the gateway — 'New chat' cannot work
bugs.component: edge-gateway route table / axis6 topology mapping
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: A valid access token for account A; a second account B.
steps: POST http://localhost:8080/conversations/dm {a:<A>, b:<B>} with A's bearer token.
POST http://localhost:3002/conversations/dm with the same body and token (identity-service's own origin).
bugs.expected: Both succeed. The client only ever talks to the gateway, so the gateway route must work.
bugs.actual: Through the gateway: 404 {message:'Cannot POST /conversations/dm', path:'/conversations/dm'}. Direct to identity-service on :3002: 201 {conversationId:'dm-…', created:true}. The gateway route table sends /conversations/dm to the GROUP_CHANNEL logical service (routes.ts:32), which under the axis6 profile does not resolve to the service that mounts ChannelsController.
bugs.user_impact: Starting a new DM is impossible through the documented client base URL — the app's entire 'New chat' flow dead-ends.
bugs.suspected_cause: A topology mapping gap for GROUP_CHANNEL under SPLIT_PROFILE=axis6. The same class of defect is already documented in the repo for /status ('The combined presence|status rule sent these to realtime, where no StatusController exists, so the whole API 404'd under axis6/full13 and only worked under mono' — routes.ts:41-43).
bugs.notes: QA/lib/provision.js works around this by falling back to the identity-service origin, so downstream chat tests are not blocked. The workaround is documented in the file.

bugs.title: Sign-out's authenticated calls ship with no Authorization header, so the server-side push endpoint is never cleared
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: A signed-in session with a registered push endpoint.
steps: Sign out.
Observe the outbound POST /auth/logout and POST /notifications/endpoints (clear) requests.
bugs.expected: Both carry `Authorization: Bearer <access>` — the code comments at authStore.ts:83-88, pushService.ts:521-522, infra/push/api.ts:34-36 and pushRuntime.ts:162-163 all state they are sent 'while the token is still valid'.
bugs.actual: clearSession() (authStore.ts:89) is synchronous, while axios 1.18.1 runs a non-`{synchronous:true}` request interceptor in a microtask. So the interceptor at client.ts:226-246 reads `auth.accessToken` AFTER clearSession() has deleted it, and both fire-and-forget calls reach the server unauthenticated. The server-side push endpoint row is never cleared.
bugs.user_impact: A signed-out device keeps receiving push wake-ups for the account that signed out, and the refresh family is not revoked server-side.
bugs.suspected_cause: Microtask ordering between a synchronous storage clear and an async axios interceptor.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by code reading (axios Axios.js:161-189 gates synchronous interceptor execution on the `synchronous` flag, which is not set).
bugs.notes: FIX: The request interceptor is now registered with {synchronous:true} (client.ts), so axios invokes it INLINE at the moment a request is issued instead of deferring it into a microtask. A call fired immediately before a synchronous clearSession() now reads the still-current token, closing the race. Verified: full jest suite 454/454 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: Sign-out then sign-in in one process silently destroys every notification action
bugs.frequency: Always after a sign-out/sign-in without killing the app
bugs.preconditions: The app has been signed in, then signed out, then signed in again — all without a process restart.
steps: Sign in, confirm push works (reply from a notification succeeds).
Sign out (this calls shutdownPushForSignOut -> stopPushRuntime).
Sign in again with the same or another number.
Receive a message and reply from the notification.
bugs.expected: The reply is sent, as it was before the sign-out.
bugs.actual: startPushRuntime() runs once with `[]` deps and is never called again. stopPushRuntime() removed both the push-event listener and `unsubSession` — the only thing that re-runs initPush() after a login. Meanwhile disposePush() is never called in app code (only from __resetPushForTests), so pushService's own AppState listener survives and keeps calling drainPendingEvents() on every foreground. That drains the native queue (PushStore.kt:403-407 deletes it) into an EMPTY eventListeners set. Every reply / mark-read / mute pressed after the re-login is drained and thrown away, and the new account never registers a push endpoint.
bugs.user_impact: Notification replies are silently lost after a re-login, and the new account gets no push at all. The user sees their reply disappear with no error.
bugs.suspected_cause: Asymmetric lifecycle: the runtime can be stopped but never restarted, and two separate dispose paths (stopPushRuntime vs disposePush) with only one of them wired.
bugs.notes: FIX: provision() now calls startPushRuntime() too (idempotent — harmless no-op on the normal first sign-in the App.tsx mount effect already started). A re-login after shutdownPushForSignOut() (sign-out) in the same process now correctly re-establishes the availability/message/session subscriptions instead of leaving them permanently torn down. Verified: full jest suite 455/455 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: Android <= 12 reports notifications as granted even when disabled, so the sync engine drops its background socket
bugs.frequency: Always on API < 33 with notifications disabled
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic by code path — NOT observable on the API 36 emulator used for this run
bugs.preconditions: An Android 10-12 device with VelChat notifications turned off in system settings.
steps: Turn off notifications for VelChat in Android system settings.
Launch the app and sign in.
Background the app.
Have another user send a message.
bugs.expected: The app detects that notifications are blocked, keeps its background socket (since push cannot wake it), and surfaces the push blocker banner.
bugs.actual: hasNotificationPermission() returns a hardcoded `true` below API 33. That feeds refreshPermission() (pushService.ts:397-399) -> isPushAvailable() true (pushState.ts:120-123) -> pushRuntime.ts:116-118 calls syncEngine.setPushAvailable(true), and the engine drops its background socket. Notifications are blocked so nothing displays either: total silence. The correct app-level check already exists natively (areNotificationsEnabled(), PushNotifications.kt:173) and is used by the banner but not by the state that gates the socket.
bugs.user_impact: On the stated reference device, a user who has notifications off receives nothing at all in the background — no notification and no socket. Messages appear only when the app is reopened.
bugs.suspected_cause: The pre-API-33 branch conflates 'no runtime permission is required' with 'notifications are enabled'.
bugs.notes: FIX: refreshPermission() (pushService.ts) trusted hasNotificationPermission() alone, which on Android <33 has no runtime dialog and unconditionally answers true regardless of the app-level or channel-level notification toggle the user can flip from system Settings. Combined it with the same native areMessageNotificationsBlocked() check the push blocker banner already used (getPushBlocker()), via a new pure decision function notificationsGranted(permitted, blocked) in pushState.ts, so permission now genuinely means the OS will show something on every API level before isPushAvailable lets the SyncEngine drop its background socket. No native code changed — reused the existing native primitive. Verified: full jest suite 456/456 pass (452 + 4 new), tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors on touched files. Could not be observed on a real Android <=12 device (none available on this machine) — the fix is verified at the unit-test level against the exact documented defect (permitted=true, blocked=true -> denied), not end-to-end on hardware.

bugs.title: clearSession() is not a session teardown — the previous account's chat DB, profile and contacts survive into the next sign-in
bugs.frequency: Always on the forced-logout path
bugs.preconditions: An active session that the server then rejects (refresh-token family revoked, e.g. after the replay in VC-014).
steps: Sign in as account A and exchange messages so the local DB, profile mirror and contact cache are populated.
Cause the server to reject the refresh token (a family revoke), so client.ts:289 calls clearSession().
Sign in with a DIFFERENT phone number.
bugs.expected: The forced-logout path performs the same teardown as signOut(): purge chat data, profile mirror, receipts, contact discovery cache, conversation-peer cache and native push state.
bugs.actual: clearSession() drops five KV keys and nothing else; authStore.sessionExpired() (authStore.ts:131-133) only flips the state. NONE of the ~15 purges signOut() performs (authStore.ts:88-123) run — no shutdownPushForSignOut, no purgeAllLocalChat, no profile-mirror delete, no KVKeys.phone delete, no clearAllReceipts/clearProfileCache/clearContactsDiscoveryCache/clearConversationPeerCache/clearStartDmCache, no native PushStore.clearSession(). The new account inherits all of it, while App.tsx:91-93 backfills the new account's inbox on top.
bugs.user_impact: Account B sees account A's chats, name, phone number, contacts and receipts. This is a cross-account data-leak on a shared or resold device.
bugs.suspected_cause: Two logout paths with different responsibilities; only the user-initiated one performs the purge.
bugs.notes: FIX: sessionExpired() now runs the same purgeAccountData() as signOut() (extracted, shared), minus clearDeviceKey() (a transient expiry must still allow a later silent relogin) and the network logout call (pointless — the session is already rejected). The next sign-in on this device, even under a different phone number, no longer inherits the previous account chat DB, profile, contacts or receipts. Verified: full jest suite 455/455 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: Rotating-refresh replay is structurally inevitable on a lost response, and the family revoke is then silently swallowed
bugs.frequency: Whenever a refresh response is lost (Render cold start, flaky network)
bugs.preconditions: A signed-in session; a refresh request whose response never arrives.
steps: Trigger a token refresh and drop the response (timeout / network loss).
doRefresh returns {status:'unavailable'} and KEEPS the refresh token the server has already rotated.
Trigger another 401 so the same refresh token is submitted again.
Cold-start the app.
bugs.expected: The client recognises that a refresh may have succeeded server-side and does not replay the same token; a family revoke forces a visible re-login.
bugs.actual: The rotated token is resubmitted, the server detects reuse and revokes the whole family (confirmed server-side by test VC-AUTH-024). The user is force-logged-out with no explanation. Because clearDeviceKey() only runs in signOut(), the next cold launch silently re-logs in via loginWithDeviceKey (useAuth.ts:286-291) — so the security signal is discarded rather than surfaced.
bugs.user_impact: Unexplained logouts on a flaky network, and a revoked-family security event that never reaches the user or telemetry.
bugs.suspected_cause: No 'this refresh token was already submitted' marker in tokens.ts.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by code reading, and the server-side family revoke is confirmed by live test VC-AUTH-024.
bugs.notes: FIX (investigated against the real backend source at D:Velchat, read-only): confirmed a refresh-reuse family revoke and a plain invalid/expired refresh both return an identical 401 UNAUTHORIZED with no distinguishing code, and confirmed device-key login is architecturally INDEPENDENT of the refresh-token family (revokeFamily only touches refresh_tokens; the devices table has no family_id) - so a device that still holds its private key can always mint a fresh session, and the client cannot and need not distinguish reuse-triggered revokes from ordinary rejections. Two real defects fixed: (1) clearSession() was deleting KVKeys.deviceId, which meant NEITHER the existing cold-start silent-relogin (useAuthBootstrap) NOR any warm recovery could ever actually reach /auth/challenge after a forced expiry, despite the code comments claiming this already worked - moved the explicit deviceId wipe into signOut() only, so a real logout is unchanged but a forced expiry now keeps it, same as the device key. (2) added attemptSilentRelogin() (authStore.ts), invoked from sessionExpired() itself, so a lost-refresh-response false-positive family revoke recovers IMMEDIATELY while the app is warm instead of only on the next cold start, turning a network hiccup back into nothing instead of stranding the user on the sign-in screen. Did not attempt to prevent the reuse-detection race itself (structurally requires a backend idempotency mechanism - out of scope, frontend-only per current instruction). Verified: full jest suite 481/481 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors. bugs.title: The cnfJkt DPoP binding is dead code — the refresh token is bound to nothing
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: Any refresh.
steps: Sign in.
Trigger a token refresh.
Inspect the outbound POST /auth/token/refresh body.
bugs.expected: `cnfJkt` carries the device key's JWK thumbprint, binding the refresh token to this device — the one piece of DPoP this backend implements.
bugs.actual: KVKeys.cnfJkt is only written by setTokens when t.cnfJkt !== undefined, and its only callers are authStore.provision (which never sets it) and doRefresh (which reads the same empty key back into itself). Every refresh sends cnfJkt: undefined. No thumbprint is computed anywhere — deviceKey.ts has no JWK/thumbprint function.
bugs.user_impact: A stolen refresh token is redeemable from any device.
bugs.suspected_cause: The binding was scaffolded but the thumbprint computation was never implemented.
bugs.notes: FIX: Added cnfJktThumbprint() (deviceKey.ts) — a real RFC 7638 JWK thumbprint (RFC 8037 OKP encoding) over the device Ed25519 public key. doRefresh() now computes it fresh on every refresh instead of round-tripping through an MMKV key nothing ever wrote a real value into. Verified: full jest suite 454/454 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: MMKV's encryption key is a hardcoded bundle constant, and the Ed25519 device private key is stored inside it
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: Read access to the APK, or filesystem access to the app's data directory.
steps: Extract the APK and read the string constant at infra/kv/mmkv.ts:10-16.
Use it to decrypt the MMKV store.
Read auth.accessToken, auth.refreshToken, auth.phone and auth.devicePrivKey.
bugs.expected: Per §L14, the device key is a non-exportable Secure Enclave / StrongBox key that only exposes sign(); tokens are protected by a key derived from the platform keystore.
bugs.actual: ENCRYPTION_KEY is the literal string 'velchat-mp0-placeholder-key-derive-from-keychain-in-mp1', compiled into every build. The store holds the access token, refresh token, cnfJkt, phone number and — via deviceKey.ts:44 — the raw Ed25519 private key as hex. That private key is exactly what POST /auth/login/device-key accepts as proof of possession.
bugs.user_impact: Anyone who can read the app's data directory obtains a permanent credential for the account: the device identity itself, which grants tokens on demand and survives a password or session reset.
bugs.suspected_cause: Deliberate MP0 placeholder — both files carry honest TODO(MP1) notes.
bugs.rootCause: The MMKV encryption key was a string literal in infra/kv/mmkv.ts, so it shipped inside every APK. Unzip, read the bundle, and you hold the key to everything the app persists at rest: the access and refresh tokens, the cnfJkt binding, and the Ed25519 device private key under auth.devicePrivKey. The last of those is the one that matters most, because it authenticates this install to the backend and cannot be re-derived — its disclosure is not something signing out can undo.
bugs.notes:
Known and tracked as MP1 work, but it is the single highest-severity item in the client and should gate any release.

FIX. A new in-app native module (com.velchat.securestore) generates 32 random bytes once per install and seals them with an AES-GCM key created in the AndroidKeyStore, which never leaves it — TEE-backed on most devices. Only the sealed blob reaches disk, so an attacker with the APK now has nothing and an attacker with the file has ciphertext. The wrapping key is deliberately NOT bound to user authentication: the store has to be readable for a push to be acknowledged behind a locked screen (M13), and a lockscreen-bound key would also be invalidated the next time the user changes their PIN, taking the device identity with it.

THE MIGRATION is the dangerous part and is what most of the design is about. An install that upgrades has its store encrypted with the old constant; opening it with the new key reads an EMPTY store, which would sign the user out and destroy the device key. So the order is: open with the legacy key, MMKV recrypt() in place, and only then does native record the key as committed. The commit is written after javascript reports success, never when the key is generated, so a process that dies mid-migration comes back uncommitted and simply tries again — opening with the new key at that point would find nothing. The decision is a pure function (resolveStoreKey) with four cases covered by tests, including that retry, because a keystore call cannot be unit-tested on this machine and getting this wrong is unrecoverable.

FAILURE IS SAFE BY DESIGN: the native side answers an empty string rather than throwing when the keystore is unusable, and javascript then stays on the legacy key. A store the app cannot open looks to a user exactly like a wiped account, which is far worse than remaining on the key the previous build already used. Nothing in either file logs a key, a blob or a fragment (M19) — only which step failed, by exception class name.

The bridge methods are synchronous on purpose: the MMKV instance is built at module scope, so the key must exist before javascript reaches its first await, or there is a legacy-encrypted window on every launch. Cost is three SharedPreferences reads and one AES-GCM operation over 32 bytes at startup.

VERIFIED ON BOTH DEVICES with real signed-in sessions, which is the only test that matters here. Emulator: migrate path — session, chats, avatars, previews and unread badges all intact after the re-encrypt; then a second cold start on the committed native key, still intact (1855 ms). Real device (OPPO CPH2643, arm64, real TEE): same, cold start 553 ms, and no keystore-fallback warning in logcat on either device, so the keystore path genuinely ran rather than silently falling back. 588/588 jest, tsc clean, eslint 0 errors, Kotlin compiles.

STILL OPEN, deliberately and recorded rather than quietly skipped: (a) iOS has no native half — the TS wrapper degrades to the legacy key there, and nothing about iOS is claimed as verified since it cannot be built on this machine. (b) The Ed25519 private key is now protected at rest but still passes through JS memory when it signs. Moving the key itself INTO the keystore, so signing happens natively and the private bytes never enter the bundle heap, is the stronger fix and is its own piece of work. (c) No new dependency was added, so no ADR was required under M1.

bugs.title: Message plaintext and the user's own typed replies persist in plaintext SharedPreferences
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: Notifications received; a reply typed from a notification.
steps: Receive several messages so notification lines accumulate.
Reply from a notification.
Read the app's SharedPreferences file.
bugs.expected: No personal message content at rest in plaintext; §M0 forbids plaintext of personal (E2EE) content in the DB or logs.
bugs.actual: KEY_LINES stores up to 6 lines x 20 conversations of message bodies; KEY_PENDING stores up to 64 queued events including reply text. EncryptedSharedPreferences was deliberately declined, with a header comment justifying it for the FCM token — which does not address personal content. showOwnReply (PushNotifications.kt:451-455) writes the user's freshly typed message, which the E2EE path would never otherwise put on disk unencrypted. cancelAll (PushNotifications.kt:533-536) clears counts but not KEY_LINES, so the content outlives the visible notification.
bugs.user_impact: Message content readable from device storage after the notification is dismissed.
bugs.suspected_cause: The storage decision was made for the token and extended to content without re-evaluation.
bugs.notes:
Needs an ADR or, at minimum, a scrub-on-cancel.

FIX: the notification store now seals its CONTENT entries at rest with the same AndroidKeyStore-wrapped key introduced for VC-016. Five entries are protected — the MessagingStyle message bodies, the pending-event queue (which holds the reply the user typed into a notification while the app was dead), the conversation and person display names, and the avatar map, because those carry URLs and on-disk paths tied to a person. Counts, seq watermarks, mute-untils, seen-seqs and the active conversation id stay plain on purpose: they are numbers and opaque ids, and sealing them would put an AES operation on the notification hot path for nothing (activeConversationId alone is read on every inbound push).

The upgrade needs no migration pass and no flag: a sealed value carries a v1: prefix, so a value without one is recognised as a legacy plaintext entry, returned as-is, and re-sealed the next time that entry is written. Sealing that fails stores the plaintext rather than dropping it — losing a queued reply is worse than storing it the way the previous build already did — and an unseal that fails returns empty, which every caller already treats as a corrupt entry rather than wedging notifications. Nothing logs a key, a blob or a fragment (M19).

Verified: Kotlin compiles clean, 588/588 jest, tsc clean, eslint 0 errors. NOT yet re-verified on a device end-to-end after the seal landed, so the live notification path under sealed storage is still owed a two-device run.

TEST-ID CORRECTION: this entry named VC-SEC-102, which does not exist anywhere in the repo. Removed rather than left standing — a testId that names nothing is worse than an empty one, because it reads as coverage. This project has no Kotlin test source set at all, so this entry is code-review-verified only.

bugs.title: No certificate pinning anywhere, in JS or native
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: A compromised or rogue system CA.
steps: Search the repo for pinning configuration.
Check android/app/src/main/res/xml/ for a networkSecurityConfig.
bugs.expected: §A1/§D4 require certificate pinning with a stapled fallback.
bugs.actual: No pinning, no TrustKit; android/app/src/main/res/xml/ does not exist. The native ack path (PushAckClient.kt:196-244, raw HttpURLConnection) has no pinning either and would need it separately.
bugs.user_impact: A rogue system CA can read tokens, OTPs and phone numbers. Apps targeting API >= 24 already exclude user-added CAs, so a casual MITM proxy is blocked — the exposure is a compromised system CA.
bugs.suspected_cause: Not yet implemented.
bugs.notes:
Grouped with VC-019: four of the five §A1/§D4 controls have no implementation.

PARTIAL — the MECHANISM ships, deliberately with ZERO pins. A platform network-security-config is declared in the manifest, which the OS enforces on every TLS socket in the process: the axios path, the WebSocket, and the killed-app PushAckClient raw HttpURLConnection are all covered by one declaration with no code on any request path. Hosts for all three flavors are listed from the .env files. NO PIN IS SHIPPED and none will be guessed: a pin only exists on a live certificate, and a wrong one brands every install permanently unreachable. NOTE the empty <pin-set> elements the first version carried had to be REMOVED — Android lint treats an empty pin-set as a FATAL error in a release build, so the app could not be assembled at all; absent and empty are identical at runtime. WHAT THE OWNER MUST SUPPLY before this can close: (1) what to pin for prod — velchat.duckdns.org is Caddy + Lets Encrypt, which rotates its key on every renewal by default, so pinning the leaf is a dead app roughly every 60 days; either pin the issuing CA SPKI or get a committed fixed key plus a published offline backup, which is a backend commitment not a client choice; (2) confirmation of the stage hosts, which .env.stage marks as placeholders in its own comments; (3) reconciliation of a contradiction — backend-integration-reference says prod is per-service on Render, .env.prod says a single Azure origin. A tripwire test asserts a backup pin and an expiry are mandatory, so the day a lone or non-expiring pin lands the board goes red. SIDE EFFECT: once a network-security-config exists, usesCleartextTraffic is ignored on minSdk 24+, so cleartext is restated there — denied except loopback and the emulator host aliases. Running Metro over a LAN IP instead of adb reverse now needs that IP added. ADR 0009.

bugs.title: Threat-model controls absent: no FLAG_SECURE, no Play Integrity, no clipboard auto-clear, no root signal
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: None.
steps: Search for FLAG_SECURE, Play Integrity / App Attest, clipboard clearing and root detection.
bugs.expected: The §A1/§D4 controls are present, especially screenshot protection on the phone-entry and OTP screens.
bugs.actual: None of the four are implemented.
bugs.user_impact: OTP and phone-entry screens are screenshottable and appear in the recents thumbnail; enrollment has no device-integrity signal.
bugs.suspected_cause: Not yet implemented.
bugs.notes:
Stated as coverage, not as a regression.

PARTIAL, each of the four decided separately (ADR 0010). CLIPBOARD AUTO-CLEAR: shipped, 60s, one timer replaced per copy, disposer returned, no new dependency. Nothing in src writes to the clipboard today, so the helper exists so the first copy feature uses the clearing path — wiring a call site is still owed. ROOT/EMULATOR: shipped as a SIGNAL only, never a gate — no blocked field and no path that refuses anything; the raw Build values are thrown away and only closed lower-case reason codes leave the module, with a test asserting no device-identifying substring can escape (M19). FLAG_SECURE: mechanism shipped, DEFAULT OFF, and turning it on is the product owner call — WhatsApp does not set it globally, it aims at the wrong adversary (it stops the screenshot path, not a camera), and it would black out the recents thumbnail and break the screenshot-driven QA this project runs on both devices. What A1 actually wants is per-screen (phone entry, OTP), which needs a JS-callable module. PLAY INTEGRITY: NOT shipped, blocked — it needs a Play Console project and cloud number (this repo has no google-services.json for dev/stage), a backend verifier endpoint that the integration reference does not expose, and a policy for a failed verdict. Adding the dependency now would ship a call that always fails and a control that looks present in a security review while verifying nothing.

bugs.title: Concurrent applyServerMessages duplicates every row in the overlap, and can lose a whole batch on a conversation PK clash
bugs.frequency: Whenever two applies overlap on one conversation
bugs.preconditions: A reconnect that starts resyncAll() while a gapped live frame triggers a gap probe on the same conversation.
steps: Force a reconnect so resyncAll() begins (SyncEngine.ts:677, no single-flight guard).
Deliver a live message frame with a seq gap on a conversation resyncAll is already applying, so the gap probe calls backfillConversation() (SyncEngine.ts:751).
Inspect the messages table for the overlapping range.
bugs.expected: One row per message. The codebase documents this exact hazard at SyncEngine.ts:192-198 and guards loadOlderMessages with `loadingOlder`.
bugs.actual: The dedup snapshot is read OUTSIDE db.write (messages.ts:202-232 vs :234). WatermelonDB serialises writers, so two overlapping applies each conclude the same rows are new and both insert them. For a new DM both also prepareCreate the same conversation PK (messages.ts:311); the second batch is rejected and ALL of its messages are lost, logged only as 'resync conversation failed' (SyncEngine.ts:1009).
bugs.user_impact: Duplicate message bubbles after a reconnect, or a silently missing block of messages in a newly created DM.
bugs.suspected_cause: Read-modify-write across the transaction boundary; the guard that exists for loadOlderMessages was not applied to resyncAll, backfillConversation or the content-fill path.
bugs.notes: VC-001 makes this far more likely to be hit in practice, because seq gaps are constant. FIX: The three lookup queries in applyServerMessages moved inside db.write(), read before any prepareCreate/prepareUpdate call — closes the race without violating the prepare-then-batch-synchronously constraint. Verified: full jest suite 454/454 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: applyReceipt is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so blue ticks can regress to grey
bugs.frequency: Whenever two receipt applications race
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic given the interleaving; invisible when applied sequentially
bugs.preconditions: Two receipt applications in flight for the same conversation.
steps: Arrange for a `read` receipt and a late `delivered` receipt to be applied concurrently (SyncEngine.ts:485, :842 and useMessages.ts:79 all call applyReceipt without awaiting each other).
Observe the stored message state.
bugs.expected: Receipt state is monotonic: delivered -> read, never backwards.
bugs.actual: Monotonicity lives ONLY in the query predicate Q.where('state', Q.oneOf(behind)), evaluated at fetch time (messages.ts:480-489) — outside the db.write at :491. Three independent un-awaited callers race, so a late `delivered` can be applied on top of a `read`.
bugs.user_impact: A blue double tick turns back to grey.
bugs.suspected_cause: The monotonic guard is in the read, not in the write.
bugs.notes: Every existing receipt test applies receipts sequentially, which is exactly why they all pass. FIX: applyReceipt now re-fetches the rows to update from inside db.write() (same pattern as VC-020) instead of before it, so the monotonic check is atomic with the write. Verified: full jest suite 454/454 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: A SendAck with seq 0 leaves the message permanently un-tickable and permanently duplicated
bugs.frequency: Whenever an ack omits or zeroes seq
bugs.preconditions: A SendAck whose seq field is missing or 0.
steps: Send a message and have the ack arrive without a usable seq (normalizeSendAck applies `pickNum(d,'seq') ?? 0`).
Observe the local row and the tick state over time.
bugs.expected: An ack without a seq is treated as a failure, or the row is repaired by the cursor backfill.
bugs.actual: seq 0 is written unconditionally (messages.ts:373) and the state flips to `sent`, so it looks fine. But the `seq > 0` filters at messages.ts:444 and :485 make the row invisible to the cursor and it can never be ticked again; the dup-destroy at :356 will not collapse the WS echo, leaving a permanent duplicate bubble.
bugs.user_impact: A message stuck at one grey tick forever, shown twice.
bugs.suspected_cause: A defaulting `?? 0` where the absence of a seq should be an error.
bugs.notes: normalizeSendAck has no test file at all. FIX: The outbox drain now rejects a SendAck with no usable seq (ack.seq is not > 0) as a retryable server-kind AppError instead of writing it as a successful send — routes through the exact same retry path as any other transient send failure, so the row never gets stuck permanently un-tickable/duplicated. Verified: full jest suite 455/455 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: One 401 on send turns the entire outbox into permanently failed messages
bugs.frequency: Whenever a send hits 401/403 with a queue behind it
bugs.preconditions: Several queued messages and an access token the server rejects.
steps: Queue 5 messages offline.
Come back online with a token the server 401s.
Observe every queued message.
bugs.expected: A 401 pauses the drain, refreshes, and retries — a transient auth problem must not destroy queued user content.
bugs.actual: The policy maps `auth` to {permanent:true, pauseDrain:false}, so the walk continues and every queued item hits the same 401 and is marked permanently failed. Every message becomes a red bubble. Note client.ts:286-288 explicitly says a refresh that could not reach the server leaves the session valid and should surface a RETRYABLE error — the outbox policy does the opposite.
bugs.user_impact: A whole queue of unsent messages is destroyed by one transient auth failure — the classic overnight-background shape.
bugs.suspected_cause: Policy choice, not an accident: sendFailurePolicy.test.ts:52 asserts this behaviour.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by code reading. This is a deliberate policy that should be revisited, not a regression.
bugs.notes: FIX: classifySendFailure() grouped auth with client, treating a post-refresh-failure 401/403 as if THIS message were rejected (permanent:true, pauseDrain:false) — one transient auth hiccup then permanently failed every other queued message as the drain kept walking into the same 401. auth is a SESSION problem, not a message problem (client.ts already treats a refresh that cannot reach the server as retryable, leaving the session valid). Added a dedicated auth case returning {permanent:false, pauseDrain:true, cooldownMs:0}, matching the network/timeout/server treatment, so the drain pauses instead of destroying the queue and resumes once the session recovers. Split the existing it.each(['client','auth']) test (which encoded the old, wrong grouping) into client-only plus a new dedicated describe block for auth. Verified: full jest suite 452/452 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: Migration-v3's five composite indexes never exist on a fresh install
bugs.frequency: Always on a fresh install
bugs.preconditions: A brand-new install (no prior schema version).
steps: Install fresh.
Inspect the SQLite schema for messages_window_idx and the other four composite indexes.
bugs.expected: The indexes exist on every install — they back subscription queries that re-run on every write to their table.
bugs.actual: A new DB takes the `schema_needed` path -> _setUpWithSchema, which emits only per-column `isIndexed` DDL. The composite indexes are created only by the v3 MIGRATION, so only UPGRADED installs have them — the inverse of what is wanted.
bugs.user_impact: Slower list queries on exactly the devices the §M0 budgets target, and a performance profile that differs between a fresh install and an upgrade.
bugs.suspected_cause: Index creation placed in a migration rather than in the schema definition.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by code reading (WatermelonDB adapters/sqlite/index.js:143-144,199; encodeSchema/index.js:22).
bugs.notes: FIX: added an unsafeSql hook to schema.ts (appSchema) — WatermelonDB's own supported extension point, confirmed by reading adapters/sqlite/encodeSchema/index.js (encodeSchema calls unsafeSql(sql, "setup") for a fresh install) — that appends the same five composite CREATE INDEX statements the v3 migration already applies on an upgrade. Extracted the five statements into a new shared compositeIndexes.ts so migrations.ts and schema.ts can never drift apart, and migrations.ts now maps over that same array instead of repeating the SQL inline. Verified: full jest suite 481/481 pass (3 new tests in schema.test.ts assert the hook exists, appends every composite index on kind:"setup", and leaves other DDL kinds untouched), tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: reassertReceipts() on every connect emits an unbounded burst the gateway silently drops
bugs.frequency: Every connect with more than ~40 owed conversations
bugs.preconditions: Many conversations owing receipts (e.g. after an overnight background).
steps: Accumulate owed receipts across 50+ conversations.
Reconnect.
Count the receipt frames sent in the first tick and what the server accepted.
bugs.expected: Receipts are chunked within the server's inbound budget, and a dropped frame is retried.
bugs.actual: All `rcpt.sent.*` markers are deleted and every owed conversation is flushed in one unchunked tick. The gateway's DEFAULT_INBOUND_PER_SECOND is 40 (ws-fabric.ts:57) and over-budget frames are DROPPED with only a warn log (ws-fabric.ts:165-168). noteSent then records them as delivered because socket.send() only checks readyState. This self-inflicts the exact backpressure receiptLedger.ts:7-9 was written to avoid.
bugs.user_impact: After a long background, the peer's ticks stay grey for most conversations, and the client believes it has already sent those receipts.
bugs.suspected_cause: No chunking and no send-confirmation on the reassert path.
testIds: failureScenarios.test.ts: receipt reassertion after a reconnect with many owed conversations
bugs.notes: FIX: flushReceipts() (SyncEngine.ts) sent one frame per owed conversation in a single synchronous tick on every reconnect reassert, with no cap — the gateway silently drops inbound frames past ~40/sec per connection (ws-fabric.ts), and the client never learns which ones were dropped since socket.send() only checks readyState, so noteSent() recorded them all as delivered regardless. Added a per-tick cap (MAX_RECEIPT_FRAMES_PER_FLUSH=20, comfortably under the shared 40/sec budget) and, when a flush goes over budget, re-marks the remaining conversations dirty and reschedules a continuation chunk 1100ms later (longer than the gateway rate-limit window, so consecutive chunks land in separate windows) via the existing scheduleReceiptFlush/receiptTimer machinery. Nothing is ever dropped, only spread across more ticks. Verified: full jest suite 485/485 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors. Added 2 new tests (failureScenarios.test.ts) with 60 owed conversations (past the real ~40/sec budget): the first synchronous flush stays under 60, and every owed receipt eventually goes out across later chunks.

bugs.title: Unread count climbs and the read watermark stalls for messages backfilled into the chat you are reading
bugs.frequency: Every reconnect while a chat is open
bugs.preconditions: Sitting in an open chat when a reconnect triggers a backfill.
steps: Open a chat.
Force a reconnect so pageBackfill runs for that conversation.
Observe the unread badge and the peer's ticks.

bugs.title: 'Load older' dead-ends permanently on a deletion hole wider than one page
bugs.frequency: Whenever a deleted run exceeds the page size
bugs.preconditions: A conversation with a contiguous run of deleted messages wider than the page limit.
steps: Delete more than one page worth of consecutive messages.
Scroll up in that conversation and keep requesting older messages.
bugs.expected: Pagination steps past the hole and keeps loading.
bugs.actual: `fresh.length === 0 -> return false`, which the UI reads as end-of-history (useMessages.ts:55). The backend's history filters deleted:false (chat.repository.ts:130), so permanent seq holes are normal — that is gapDetection.ts's whole premise.
bugs.user_impact: Older history becomes permanently unreachable in the UI even though it exists on the server.
bugs.suspected_cause: An empty page is treated as end-of-history rather than as a hole to step over.
testIds: failureScenarios.test.ts: loading older history across a wide deletion hole
bugs.notes: FIX: fetchOlderMessages() (SyncEngine.ts) treated an empty page from the server as end-of-history, but the backend filters deleted:false — a contiguous deleted run wider than one page comes back completely empty even though real history exists further back. Since the UI (useMessages.ts) only grows its window when loadOlderMessages returns true, and only fires another load on a scroll past a NEW oldest bubble, a false end-of-history report is a permanent dead end with no way for the user to retry. Converted the single fetch into a loop that steps the cursor back over an empty page and tries again, up to a generous safety cap (MAX_HOLE_HOPS=200, purely a circuit breaker against a pathological/corrupt history) before genuinely giving up. One loadOlderMessages() call now reaches all the way past a hole (or to the true start of history) in one go. Verified: full jest suite 485/485 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors. Added 2 new tests (failureScenarios.test.ts) with a 70-message-wide deletion hole (wider than the 50-message page): one call steps past it and loads the older page, and the true end-of-history case is unaffected.

bugs.title: No event_id dedup anywhere — the documented at-least-once guard does not exist
bugs.frequency: Whenever the server redelivers an event
bugs.preconditions: A redelivered durable event (the bus is at-least-once).
steps: Search the client for an event_id LRU or dedup set.
Redeliver the same message frame twice.
bugs.expected: An event_id LRU rejects the duplicate, as the doc comment at socket.ts:7 implies.
bugs.actual: No dedup structure exists anywhere in the client. Dedup relies entirely on the DB's client_msg_id/seq paths, which VC-020 shows are not race-safe.
bugs.user_impact: Duplicate bubbles on redelivery.
bugs.suspected_cause: Documented but never implemented.
bugs.notes: NO CODE CHANGE — not reproducible as filed; closing with evidence rather than building the suggested LRU. Two points. (1) The premise has been overtaken: the report says dedup relies on DB client_msg_id/seq paths "which VC-020 shows are not race-safe" — VC-020 was fixed earlier in this run (the batch lookups were moved INSIDE db.write, making check-and-act atomic), so those paths ARE now race-safe. (2) The reported impact (duplicate bubbles on redelivery) is already covered by passing tests: failureScenarios.test.ts "a duplicate realtime frame produces one row, one unread and one preview — however many times it lands" delivers the IDENTICAL frame three times and asserts a single row, and "does not duplicate when a whole catch-up is replayed" re-serves an entire window. Also note socket.ts:7 does not promise an LRU — it documents where event_id LIVES in the envelope, not that the client indexes it. An event_id LRU would be a second, redundant dedup layer in front of one the database already provides idempotently (seq is the server-assigned identity), with its own memory and eviction to get wrong. Recommend reopening only if a real duplicate is ever observed on a device.

bugs.title: Outbox backoff exhaustion is unreachable — MAX_SEND_ATTEMPTS can never fire
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: A message that keeps failing.
steps: Force repeated send failures.
Check whether attempt-count exhaustion is ever consulted.
bugs.expected: After MAX_SEND_ATTEMPTS the message is marked failed by exhaustion.
bugs.actual: outbox.ts:281-286 is only consulted when `permanent === undefined`, and SyncEngine.ts:1156 always passes a boolean — so the branch is dead. syncLogic.test.ts:96-113 tests dead code.
bugs.user_impact: Retry behaviour differs from the documented policy; a message can retry indefinitely on a classification the policy treats as retryable.
bugs.suspected_cause: A call-site refactor left the exhaustion branch unreachable.
bugs.notes: FIX: removed the dead attempt-count exhaustion path (MAX_SEND_ATTEMPTS/nextOutboxRetry in syncLogic.ts) that markFailed() fell back to only when permanent was omitted — a fallback no real call site ever triggered (SyncEngine.ts always passes a classified boolean from classifySendFailure()). This mechanism contradicted the documented WhatsApp-style policy (sendFailurePolicy.ts: reachability failures retry forever, never auto-fail by attempt count) and had no basis in the HLD/LLD spec (§L6 outbox semantics: classification-based retryable-vs-permanent only, no attempt cap). Made markFailed()'s permanent parameter required (compiler now prevents the dead path from ever coming back), updated the one test that accidentally relied on the old default (realtime-hardening.test.ts) to pass permanent explicitly, removed the 4 tests for the deleted dead function, and added a new regression test proving a retryable cause stays queued past a high attempt count. Verified: full jest suite 452/452 pass (455 - 4 removed + 1 added), tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: Message window sorts by created_at, not seq — a device clock ahead of the server permanently mis-orders own messages
bugs.device: any Android with a skewed clock
bugs.frequency: Whenever the device clock leads the server
bugs.preconditions: Device clock set ahead of the server.
steps: Set the device clock 10 minutes ahead.
Send messages and receive replies.
Observe the order in the chat.
bugs.expected: Ordering is by seq. The backend is explicit: 'sort by seq, never timestamp' (backend-integration-reference.md §5).
bugs.actual: The window query sorts by created_at, so a locally stamped own message sorts after later server messages and stays there.
bugs.user_impact: Messages appear in the wrong order and never correct themselves.
bugs.suspected_cause: The window query orders by the local timestamp rather than the server seq.
testIds: messageOrdering.test.ts: VC-030 — a device clock running ahead of the server
bugs.notes: FIX: two causes, both in the created_at-as-sort-key design. (1) markMessageSent() re-stamped createdAt to the server clock FORWARD ONLY (if (ack.serverTs > m.createdAt)), a rule meant to stop a slow server clock re-burying an offline-composed bubble. Forward-only mixes two clocks in one sort key: on a device whose clock leads the server, an own message keeps its future local stamp and beats every server timestamp that follows it, permanently. The server clock is the same authority that assigns seq, so its timestamp is now adopted in EITHER direction. (2) messageWindowClauses() (extracted from observeMessages so the real query is testable rather than duplicated in a test) now sorts by created_at DESC then seq DESC — seq is the ordering identity per backend-integration-reference §5, and the gateway fans bursts out inside one millisecond, so identical created_at values are normal and were previously resolved by whatever order rows happened to be written. seq is the SECOND key, not the first, because an unsent message has no seq and sorting on it first would file every pending bubble under a null and drag it out of the newest-first window. The pre-existing test never drags a message backwards in time encoded the defect; it was rewritten to assert the concern it actually cared about — that a backwards re-stamp does not change the bubble POSITION — which now holds because seq decides the order. Verified: full jest suite 492/492 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: runQueuedPushActions runs queued notification actions concurrently while claiming to serialize them
bugs.frequency: Whenever two or more actions are queued
bugs.preconditions: Two replies queued from notifications while the app was killed.
steps: Queue two notification replies.
Foreground the app so the queue drains.
Observe the order of the resulting sends.
bugs.expected: Sequential, each awaited — as the comment directly above the code states.
bugs.actual: `events.map(e => () => handlePushEvent(e)).map(run => run())` invokes every handler before allSettled, so all run concurrently. Two inline replies write two outbox rows and run markConversationRead concurrently inside a 30s wake window, defeating the ordering collapsePendingEvents works to preserve.
bugs.user_impact: Replies sent from notifications can arrive out of order.
bugs.suspected_cause: The double `.map` invokes eagerly; the intent was a sequential reduce.
bugs.notes: FIX: the drain mapped each queued event to a thunk and then IMMEDIATELY mapped again to call it — events.map(e => () => handle(e)).map(run => run()) — so every handler was already in flight before Promise.allSettled waited on anything. The code did the exact opposite of the comment directly above it. Replaced with a new runSequentially() helper (features/notifications/model) that awaits each action in turn while still collecting per-item outcomes, so one failing action cannot abandon the rest (a reply must go out even if a preceding mute threw) — allSettle gives that second property but cannot give the first, since it can only wait on promises that have already been started. Verified: full jest suite 506/506 pass (4 new tests, including a max-concurrency assertion that fails against the old eager implementation), tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: No duplicate-notification suppression, though the monotonic watermark to do it already exists
bugs.frequency: Whenever FCM redelivers (at-least-once)
bugs.preconditions: A push redelivered by FCM.
steps: Receive the same push twice.
Observe the notification thread and the unread count.
bugs.expected: The second delivery is suppressed by the seq watermark PushStore already maintains (PushStore.kt:172-182).
bugs.actual: showMessage calls bumpCount() and appendLine() BEFORE consulting the watermark; setLastSeq is write-only here. The thread line and the count are both doubled.
bugs.user_impact: Duplicate notification lines and an inflated unread badge.
bugs.suspected_cause: The guard was never added; the watermark is maintained but not read on this path.
bugs.notes:
The fix is one line: `if (seq > 0 && seq <= store.lastSeq(conversationId)) return false`.

FIXED, but NOT the way this entry proposed, and the difference matters. The entry says the monotonic watermark to do this already exists (PushStore.lastSeq). Suppressing on a high-water mark would be wrong here: FCM gives no ordering guarantee, and this session PROVED it out of order on a real device — the notification thread came back with KILL2 above KILL1, which is what VC-056 exists to sort. Against a watermark, a genuinely new message arriving with a LOWER seq than one already delivered would have its notification silently swallowed entirely — a far worse failure than showing a duplicate. So suppression is by EXACT identity instead: new PushStore.markSeen(conversationId, seq) records the seq and returns whether it was new, keeping the last 20 seqs per conversation (bounded, and only has to outlast FCM retries), atomic under the same WRITE_LOCK. handleMessage calls it BEFORE the on-screen check, so a duplicate of a message the user already watched arrive in an open chat cannot notify later either. Everything after it still runs for a duplicate on purpose: the delivered ack is idempotent and re-acking guarantees the sender their tick, and handing the push to a live JS runtime is a free chance to catch up. Cleared on sign-out with the rest of the session state. Verified by compileProdReleaseKotlin; no Kotlin test source set exists, and an FCM redelivery cannot be forced on demand, so this is code-review-verified.

bugs.title: Native pending-event queue is a lock-free read-modify-write that can wipe a reply enqueued mid-drain
bugs.frequency: Whenever an enqueue overlaps a drain
bugs.preconditions: A push arriving on the FCM thread while JS drains the queue on the native-modules thread.
steps: Start a drain.
Have a push enqueue an event during the drain.
Check whether the new event survives.
bugs.expected: Each queued entry is handed to exactly one caller and nothing is lost — which is what the JS side asserts at pushService.ts:190-191 and relies on to skip single-flighting.
bugs.actual: enqueueEvent and takeEvents are unsynchronized, and takeEvents does `prefs.edit().remove(KEY_PENDING)` — deleting the WHOLE key rather than the drained prefix. An event enqueued mid-drain is wiped.
bugs.user_impact: A reply typed from a notification can silently vanish.
bugs.suspected_cause: No synchronization and a whole-key delete instead of a prefix removal.
bugs.notes:
No JVM test source set exists — android/app/src contains only `main`. PushStore is plain-JVM-testable.

FIXED as part of VC-066. The pending-event queue is one of the read-modify-write pairs that the new companion-object WRITE_LOCK now covers: enqueueEvent reads the array, appends, trims and writes it back, and takeEvents reads it and removes the key, both entirely inside the monitor. The drain case this entry described — an action queued on the receiver thread between the read and the removal, silently dropped — can no longer interleave, and the code now carries a comment saying exactly that. The monitor is on the COMPANION object rather than the instance, which is load-bearing: PushStore is constructed fresh at each entry point (VelChatMessagingService on FCM delivery, PushActionReceiver on main, VelChatPushModule on the RN native-modules thread), so an instance monitor would have been three separate locks guarding one shared SharedPreferences file. Verified by code review plus a clean compileProdReleaseKotlin; there is no Kotlin test source set in this project, so this is code-review-verified only.
