bugs.title: Retry-After is honored with an unbounded, uncancellable sleep
bugs.frequency: Whenever a 429 carries a large Retry-After
bugs.preconditions: A response with `Retry-After: 86400`.
steps: Return a 429 with Retry-After: 86400.
Observe the request.
bugs.expected: The wait is clamped to a sane ceiling and is cancellable.
bugs.actual: `await wait(retryAfter * 1000)` with no clamp, no ceiling, no negative guard and no abort check. The axios timeout does not apply because the wait is outside the request. The setTimeout is never cleared, and a request cancelled during the wait still fires afterwards. The 5xx backoff path has the same shape.
bugs.user_impact: A request can park for 24 hours; a timer leaks (MOPS-1 reject criterion: a timer without disposal).
bugs.suspected_cause: Missing clamp and disposal.
bugs.notes: FIX: Retry-After is now clamped to [0, 10s] (MAX_RETRY_AFTER_MS, client.ts) before the wait, instead of obeying a server-supplied value unbounded. Verified: full jest suite 454/454 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: A misbuilt binary reports env:'dev' while talking to production
bugs.frequency: Whenever react-native-config fails to inject
bugs.preconditions: A build where `Config` is empty (stale/cached .env, misbuilt flavor).
steps: Build with react-native-config unable to inject.
Read the 'backend base' log line.
bugs.expected: The diagnostic tells the truth, or the app refuses to run.
bugs.actual: `name` falls back to 'dev' while `apiBaseUrl` falls back to the PROD host. client.ts:45 then logs {env:'dev', apiBaseUrl:'…duckdns.org'} — the only diagnostic for this failure mode actively lies. A debuggable APK with usesCleartextTraffic=true then points real OTP requests, phone numbers and tokens at production.
bugs.user_impact: Test traffic and real phone numbers hit production from a debug build, undetectably.
bugs.suspected_cause: Two independent fallbacks that can disagree.
bugs.notes: The prod URL fallback direction is defensible; make `name` fall back to 'prod' alongside it, or log.error when Config.API_BASE_URL is absent. FIX: Extracted the pure resolveAppEnv(rawName, rawApiBaseUrl, rawWsUrl) so the fallback logic is unit-testable. An unrecognised/missing ENV now falls back to 'prod' alongside the URL fallback (previously 'dev'), so a misbuilt binary can never report a safe-sounding name while actually pointing at production. Verified: full jest suite 455/455 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: Cold start after >15 min idle opens the WebSocket with a certainly-expired token
bugs.frequency: Every cold start after 15+ min idle
bugs.preconditions: A stored access token older than its 900s TTL.
steps: Sign in.
Leave the app closed for 20 minutes.
Cold start and watch the WebSocket handshake.
bugs.expected: The token is refreshed before the socket is opened.
bugs.actual: hasSession() is `Boolean(getAccessToken())` — true for an EXPIRED token — so bootstrap hydrates and never refreshes. SyncEngine.ts:449-451 hands the dead token to socket.connect. Recovery exists (4001 -> refresh -> reconnect), so it is not silent, but every such cold start costs a guaranteed failed handshake plus a refresh plus a reconnect.
bugs.user_impact: Slower first sync on every cold start after idle, and avoidable battery/network cost on the reference device.
bugs.suspected_cause: hasSession() checks presence, not validity. accessTokenExpiresInMs() already exists and is used by the push runtime but not here.
bugs.notes: FIX: hasValidSession() added (tokens.ts); useAuthBootstrap now refreshes before hydrating on an expired-but-present token. hasSession() deliberately left presence-only to protect SyncEngine reconnect guards. Verified: full jest suite 454/454 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors.

bugs.title: The access token travels in the WebSocket query string
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: Any realtime connection.
steps: Open the socket.
Inspect the connect URL.
bugs.expected: The token rides the `Authorization` header, which the backend already accepts.
bugs.actual: It is appended as `?token=`. Query strings land in every proxy/CDN access log along the path (Caddy on the Azure VM, Render's edge). The stated justification — 'RN's WebSocket can't set headers reliably' — is weaker than it reads: RN's WebSocket constructor accepts a third {headers} argument on both platforms.
bugs.user_impact: Access tokens accumulate in server access logs.
bugs.suspected_cause: A platform limitation that no longer holds.
testIds: socket.test.ts: hands the token to the transport as an Authorization header
socket.test.ts: leaves the connect URL byte-identical to the configured one
bugs.notes:
The one leak-into-logs path in the client itself is already mitigated by redact.ts's JWT pattern.

FIXED. The token now rides Authorization: Bearer and the URL is left byte-identical to the configured one. The old justification in the file — RN WebSocket cannot set headers reliably — was simply wrong: RN takes a third options argument with headers on both platforms, and the gateway has read req.headers.authorization since /ws first shipped (verified in D:/Velchat libs/feature-realtime/src/fabric/ws-fabric.ts and its spec, which has a case titled accepts the token from an Authorization header as well as the query string). NO ?token= fallback is kept: a hedge that is sent on every connect is not a fallback, it IS the leak, and there is no older deployment to hedge against since the gateway read the header first all along. The one failure mode this leaves — a runtime that drops the headers argument — surfaces as a 4001, which the engine already survives with refresh-and-reconnect. Seven socket tests cover the header, the clean URL, a base URL that already has query params, and that a RECONNECT authenticates with the token it is handed rather than the one it first saw. DEVICE CONNECT TEST STILL OWED: this needs one real connect against the live gateway, which the session owner runs.

bugs.title: Jest reports a worker that failed to exit gracefully — a leaked timer or handle in the test path
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: None.
steps: Run `pnpm --filter @velchat/mobile test`.
Read the final lines of output.
bugs.expected: The suite exits cleanly.
bugs.actual: 'A worker process has failed to exit gracefully and has been force exited. This is likely caused by tests leaking due to improper teardown.' All 450 tests pass, so this is hygiene rather than a failure — but §M7 requires every long-lived resource to be owned and disposable, and this is the signal that one is not.
bugs.user_impact: None directly. It masks real leak regressions and slows CI.
bugs.suspected_cause: An undisposed timer or listener in a module the suite imports (the push/sync modules arm intervals at import time).
bugs.rootCause: Unknown — requires engineering investigation. Run with --detectOpenHandles to localise.
bugs.notes: FIX (root cause found by instrumentation, not guesswork): --detectOpenHandles reported NOTHING, so the leak was invisible to it. A probe dumping process.getActiveResourcesInfo() in afterAll showed four live Timeouts while _getActiveHandles() was empty. Traced to WatermelonDB: adapters/lokijs/worker/lokiExtensions.js constructs the Loki database with autosave:true, autosaveInterval:500 — a 500ms setInterval that is only ever cleared by loki.close(), which the app never calls because its database lives for the life of the process. Correct in production (which uses the real native SQLite adapter and never sees this code) but under Jest that interval outlives the run and holds the worker event loop open. Fixed at the source by passing extraLokiOptions:{autosave:false} to the LokiJSAdapter mock in jest.setup.ts — a first-class documented adapter option that WatermelonDB spreads AFTER its own defaults, so it overrides them; there is nothing to autosave in an in-memory adapter that starts fresh every run. MEASURED before/after with the same command: a DB-touching suite went from never exiting (killed at 90-120s, exit 124) to exit 0, and the full suite from blowing past a 120s timeout to completing and exiting in ~18s — --forceExit is no longer needed. RESIDUAL, stated honestly: the "worker process has failed to exit gracefully" text can still appear with >=2 jest workers. That is worker-pool teardown timing, not a leak in our test code — verified by the warning being absent at --maxWorkers=1 (35s) and absent for every heavy suite run individually (failureScenarios, restart, realtime-hardening all clean), while present at --maxWorkers=2 (19s) and 4 (12s). Verified: full jest suite 506/506 pass, tsc --noEmit clean, eslint clean.

bugs.title: Any authenticated user can READ and WRITE any conversation — no authorization on the chat routes, and conversation ids are derivable offline
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: One ordinary VelChat account (any account, no special role). The target conversation id, which is COMPUTED rather than guessed.
steps: Provision three accounts A, B and C. A and B open a DM; A sends "TOP SECRET between A and B".
C is not a member of that conversation and holds only its own ordinary token.

C derives the conversation id offline: "dm-" + the first 32 hex chars of sha256("<loAccountId>|<hiAccountId>"). No secret is involved (apps/mobile/src/infra/db/dmId.ts:29-38 is a byte-exact port of the backend).
C calls GET /chat/conversations/<id>/messages?afterSeq=0 with its own token.
C calls GET /conversations/<id> and GET /conversations/<id>/members.
C calls POST /chat/messages for that conversation id with its own token.
B re-reads the conversation.
bugs.expected: Every one of those calls returns 403/404 for a non-member. Authentication is not authorization: membership must gate reads, metadata, member enumeration and writes.
bugs.actual: Measured: (1) C reads the messages — 200, ["TOP SECRET between A and B"]. (2) With NO token the same call is correctly 401, so authentication IS enforced. (3) C reads conversation details — 200. (4) C enumerates the member list — 200, both account ids returned. (5) C WRITES into the DM — 201 with seq 2. (6) B then sees ["TOP SECRET between A and B","C INTRUDED HERE"]. Authorization is absent entirely on these routes.
bugs.user_impact: Any single registered user can read every private conversation in the system and inject messages that appear to the real members as part of their chat. Because the DM id is sha256 of the sorted account-id pair, no enumeration or guessing is needed — and account ids are themselves obtainable from the member list of any conversation the attacker can already reach, which is all of them. This is a complete breach of message confidentiality and integrity.
bugs.suspected_cause: The chat and conversation controllers derive the principal from the JWT (which is why impersonation via senderId is correctly rejected — see VC-SEC-021) but never check that principal against the conversation membership projection.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by live reproduction: authentication is enforced (401 without a token) while authorization is not (200/201 for a non-member holding any valid token).
bugs.notes: Highest-impact finding of the run. It also leaves E2EE as the only remaining confidentiality control — and E2EE is not implemented yet (the client still sends plaintext `content`), so there is no compensating control today.

bugs.title: A push endpoint can be registered against another account's userId, redirecting their push wake-ups
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: Two accounts A and B. B holds its own valid token.
steps: B POSTs /notifications/endpoints with its own bearer token and its own deviceId, but userId set to A's accountId and a push token B controls.
Observe the response.
bugs.expected: Rejected, or the row is bound to the token's principal (B). The client fills this userId from its own local state (apps/mobile/src/infra/push/api.ts:24-28, pushService.ts:455-460), so the server must never trust it.
bugs.actual: 201 Created. The endpoint row is accepted with a userId the caller merely asserted.
bugs.user_impact: B receives A's push wake-ups — conversation ids, message types, and previews for non-E2EE chats. Combined with VC-039 the attacker can then read the referenced messages in full.
bugs.suspected_cause: The endpoint upserts on device_id and trusts the body's userId rather than binding it to the verified token.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by live reproduction. This upgrades audit finding S7 from a suspicion to a defect.
bugs.notes: The same body-trusts-userId pattern appears in the notification prefs API and should be audited with it.

bugs.title: POST /chat/messages accepts a conversationId that does not exist
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: Any valid token.
steps: POST /chat/messages with conversationId "dm-does-not-exist-0000" and otherwise valid fields.
bugs.expected: 4xx — a message cannot belong to a conversation that does not exist.
bugs.actual: 201 Created. The message is persisted against a conversation id with no conversation row and no members.
bugs.user_impact: Unbounded writes into a table with no owner, and it is the same missing check that makes VC-039 exploitable for writes. Messages accumulate that nobody can read or moderate.

bugs.title: POST /chat/messages accepts an empty or whitespace-only message
bugs.frequency: Always
bugs.preconditions: A conversation the sender belongs to.
steps: POST /chat/messages with content "".
Repeat with "   " and with "\n\n".
bugs.expected: 4xx for each — an empty bubble is not a message.
bugs.actual: 201 Created for all three. Empty messages are persisted and fan out to the recipient.
bugs.user_impact: Empty bubbles in the conversation, and a trivial way to bump a chat to the top of the inbox with no content.

bugs.title: Concurrent refresh-token requests can all succeed — rotation is not race-safe
bugs.frequency: Observed 1/1 (3 of 3 concurrent requests succeeded)
bugs.reproducibility: Needs repeat runs to establish a rate, but reproduced on first attempt
bugs.preconditions: A valid, not-yet-rotated refresh token.
steps: Provision an identity and note its refresh token R.
Fire three POST /auth/token/refresh requests with R SIMULTANEOUSLY (Promise.all, no sequencing).
Count how many return a 2xx with a new token set.
bugs.expected: At most one request succeeds; rotation must be atomic so the first winner invalidates R for every other in-flight request. Otherwise reuse detection (VC-AUTH-024, confirmed working for a SEQUENTIAL replay) cannot do its job against a concurrent one, and the "whole family revoked on reuse" security property has a race window.
bugs.actual: All 3 of 3 concurrent requests returned a new, distinct token set. None were rejected.
bugs.user_impact: A refresh token, once briefly exposed (e.g. captured by a MITM despite TLS, or replayed from a compromised client queue), can be redeemed multiple times in the race window before the first rotation commits — defeating the single-use guarantee rotation is meant to provide.
bugs.suspected_cause: The refresh handler likely reads-then-writes the token record without a compare-and-swap or row lock across concurrent requests for the same token.
bugs.notes: Found during the 2026-09-11 re-verification pass (run verify-002), not in the original audit.

bugs.title: Contact name/contact update does not sync immediately in chat UI
bugs.frequency: Reported
bugs.reproducibility: Unconfirmed — reported from manual production testing
bugs.preconditions: A new contact is saved in the phone's contact list.
steps: Save a new contact in the phone's address book.
Open VelChat and enter that phone number / find the conversation.
Observe only the phone number is shown, not the saved contact name.
Send a message and exit the chat.
Re-check — the contact name now appears, and multiple pending contact updates appear together instead of as they happen.
bugs.expected: After saving the contact, VelChat should immediately detect/sync the contact and display the saved contact name consistently wherever that contact appears.
bugs.actual: Initially only the phone number is displayed. After opening/chatting and then exiting the chat, the contact name appears. The contact information does not update immediately, and multiple contact-related updates appear together instead of updating immediately.
bugs.user_impact: Users see raw phone numbers instead of contact names until they interact with the chat, which reads as broken contact sync.
bugs.suspected_cause: Not yet investigated.
bugs.rootCause: Not yet investigated — reported from manual production QA testing, needs code-level triage.
bugs.notes:
PARTIALLY FIXED — still open pending the remaining half. The name-precedence half is done (see VC-047): a saved contact name now wins over the registered one and resolves at READ time in the chat list and chat header, so it no longer requires opening the chat first, and a background revalidation can no longer overwrite it. What is NOT fixed, and why this stays open: the residual complaint is DISCOVERY TIMING, not precedence — a contact saved in the phone while VelChat is running is not matched until the next discovery run (app resume / prewarm), so until then that peer is genuinely unknown to the client and still renders as the number. Making that immediate needs the address-book snapshot to notify its readers (or a contacts-changed observer) so an already-mounted chat list re-renders, which is a separate change and is deliberately NOT bolted on here. Re-test after the VC-047 fix: the wrong-name-shown symptoms should be gone; only the just-saved-while-app-open case should remain.

FIXED. The residual was two things, both downstream of the VC-047 precedence fix. (1) Nothing ever asked for a re-sweep: discovery ran only at app mount, sign-in, and the New Chat screen, so a contact saved while VelChat was already running was in no sweep — the reporters workaround of sending a message and leaving the chat was just doing something else until a sweep happened to run. (2) Even a successful sweep could not reach a mounted screen: the saved name lives in the phone address book, so the conversation row never changes and there is no DB write that would re-emit it. FIX: a pure sameContactNames gate on would any DM be titled differently, a subscribeDiscoveredContacts notification fired only when that gate says a title could change, and a requestContactsRefresh with four cost gates in order — nothing to gain, 60s throttle, off the render path, and incremental so only a number with no remembered outcome goes to OPRF (one round trip, not the book). The chat list and the chat header both re-title on the notification and ask for a sweep on return to the foreground; app-returned deliberately bypasses the throttle, because another app is the only place a contact can be saved. NOT DONE: a native contacts ContentObserver, which would need an ADR. DEVICE RE-TEST STILL OWED: with a chat open showing a bare number, save that number in the phone contacts, switch back, and the title should change with nothing else touched.

bugs.title: Real-time messaging and notification-reply sync needs multi-scenario two-device verification
bugs.frequency: N/A — verification task
bugs.preconditions: Two physical devices, each signed into a separate VelChat account.
steps: Exchange messages continuously between two devices for 10-13 minutes across different messaging scenarios via the normal Chat Page.
Test notification-based replies from both devices for 6-8 minutes.
Remove both apps from the background (swipe away / kill) and reply ONLY through notifications.
Test a mixed scenario: one device replies through the notification while the other sends/replies normally from the Chat Page.
bugs.expected: Messages and replies are delivered and synchronized correctly in real time across both devices in every tested scenario, including normal Chat Page messaging, notification replies, background-removed app state, and mixed notification + Chat Page messaging.
bugs.actual: Not yet executed — result pending. Logged as a required verification pass across the scenarios above.
bugs.user_impact: Any gap here directly breaks core messaging reliability and notification-reply delivery, the two most-used flows in the app.
bugs.suspected_cause: N/A — this is a test-execution task, not yet a diagnosed defect.
bugs.notes:
This entry tracks a two-device manual verification pass, not a confirmed defect. Assigned to Tusha Bhadouriya to execute and report actual pass/fail per scenario back into this bug.

VERIFIED 2026-09-14 by a live two-device session (A = OPPO CPH2643 Android 16 real device, B = Pixel emulator Android 16), production build against the live backend. PASSED: single-message real-time delivery; an 8-message burst delivered complete and in order; notification posted with the correct sender name, avatar and per-message lines while backgrounded; notification posted after the process was killed with am kill (FCM woke the dead process and it displayed correctly); tapping a notification opens the right conversation and clears the tray; NO notification is posted while that conversation is on screen (active-conversation suppression works); inline notification Reply sends the message, clears the notification and clears the unread badge; typing indicator appears on the peer header; presence shows online and last-seen; offline send queues and flushes in order on reconnect (airplane mode on/off); unread badges and chat-list ordering correct; cold start COLD TotalTime 1367 ms. bugs.title: Online/offline presence status updates with a noticeable delay
bugs.frequency: Reported
bugs.reproducibility: Unconfirmed — reported from manual production testing
bugs.preconditions: Two users in an active/visible chat.
steps: Have the peer come online or go offline.
Observe how long the status indicator takes to reflect the change.
bugs.expected: When a user comes online or goes offline, their status should update and display immediately to other users.
bugs.actual: The user's online/offline status is displayed after a noticeable delay.
bugs.user_impact: Users see stale presence information, which can mislead them about whether the other person is actually available.
bugs.suspected_cause: Polling + server TTL, because the backend has no presence push. Not a client defect.
bugs.rootCause: Root-caused, but the fix is NOT client-side. Quantified below.
bugs.notes:
INVESTIGATED — left OPEN deliberately, no code change. The client side is already correct: activatePresence() does a LEADING await refreshPeerPresence() before it starts the interval, so there is no missing first read, and the poll is correctly scoped to the open chat and paused when suspended/offline (§M13 battery). The delay is architectural and has two additive parts. (1) There is NO live presence push to wait for: the realtime gateway FanoutConsumer subscribes to message/receipt/caption only, never presence.changed, so a presence change cannot reach a socket — this is already documented at the top of infra/network/presence.ts and is why a REST snapshot poll exists at all. (2) The numbers: peer COMES ONLINE is seen at the next poll, PEER_PRESENCE_POLL_MS = 20s, so up to ~20s. Peer GOES OFFLINE is worse, because nobody publishes a leaving event — their online:{userId} Redis key has to EXPIRE server-side (PRESENCE_ONLINE_TTL_MS = 30s from their last 20s heartbeat) and only then can our next poll observe it, so up to ~50s. That matches the reported "noticeable delay" exactly. THE REAL FIX IS BACKEND: have the gateway fan out presence.changed over the WS; the client already has the receiving path (onInboundPresence + normalizePresenceEvent are written and forward-compatible), so it would light up with no client change. The only client-side lever is lowering PEER_PRESENCE_POLL_MS, which buys latency with a REST request per interval per open chat and is a direct trade against the §R5/§R6 battery and request budgets on the 3GB reference device — a product call, not one to make silently, so it is NOT done here. Needs a decision: accept the delay, lower the poll interval (say what latency is acceptable), or schedule the backend fan-out.

LIVE CHECK 2026-09-14 (two devices, production build): presence did update — the chat header showed "online" while the peer had the app open and switched to "last seen 9:39 am" after the peer backgrounded, and the typing indicator appeared within about 2 s of the peer typing. Latency was not instrumented, so this observation does not close the report; it narrows it to a latency question rather than a functional failure.

FIXED — but not the way this entry assumed, and the earlier investigation note was wrong on one point. The architectural claim was VERIFIED against the running backend rather than the doc: the fan-out consumer subscribes to conversation, channel-member, message sent/delivered/read, contact.registered and call.caption, and there is NO presence.changed subscription — while the presence service DOES publish that event to the bus. So the event exists and the gateway simply never picks it up; the client receiving path is already written and would light up with one bus.subscribe line on the backend. CORRECTION to the earlier note: its peer-goes-offline figure only applies to an ungraceful exit; on a normal background the client posts /presence/offline immediately, so server state is right at once. THE REAL CLIENT DEFECT the earlier note missed: the open chat presence poll is torn down by every path that releases the link — network loss and the M13 background suspend both clear the timer — and NOTHING ever started it again. The only caller of activatePresence is the header mount effect, and neither returning from the background nor from a tunnel remounts a screen. A chat held open across a single interruption showed the presence it had read BEFORE the interruption for as long as the user stayed in it. Reported as updates with a delay; it was actually stops updating. FIX: resumePeerPresence re-subscribes (the server subscriber set expires after 300s), does a leading refresh and re-arms the interval, called from onForeground and from the network-restored branch. Keyed off activePresencePeers and NOT activeConversationId, because useMessages re-asserts the active id AFTER the engine handles the same transition — a resume keyed on it would no-op on the one transition that needs it most. The 20s interval is unchanged: halving it buys ~10s of average latency for a REST GET plus a subscribe POST every 10s per open chat on the 3 GB reference device (R5/R6), and still would not produce a live update. The remaining steady-state latency is backend-blocked, with the evidence above. DEVICE RE-TEST STILL OWED, observer-side: open a chat, background for 40s or toggle airplane mode, return, and confirm the peer status still tracks instead of freezing.

bugs.title: Chat List shows the registered VelChat name instead of the saved contact name until a chat is opened
bugs.component: Chat List / Message Yourself / Contact List
bugs.frequency: Reported
bugs.preconditions: A contact is saved locally under a custom name different from their VelChat registered name (e.g. saved as "Aayush Sir" for an account registered as "Aayush Jain").
steps: Save a contact's number under a custom local name that differs from their VelChat display name.
Open the Chat List — observe the registered VelChat name is shown instead of the saved contact name.
Open the contact's chat via Message Yourself and return to the Chat List.
Observe the name has now updated to the saved contact name.
bugs.expected: The saved contact name should be displayed immediately in the Chat List wherever the contact is shown, without requiring the user to open the chat first.
bugs.actual: Initially the registered VelChat name ("Aayush Jain") is displayed. After opening the contact's chat through Message Yourself and returning to the Chat List, it changes to the saved contact name ("Aayush Sir").
bugs.user_impact: Users see the wrong display name for their own saved contacts until they happen to open that specific chat, which is confusing and looks like a sync bug.
bugs.suspected_cause: Possibly the same underlying cause as the contact-sync bug reported separately — the Chat List may resolve the display name before local contact-name resolution/caching has run.
bugs.notes: FIX (root-caused): the address book was consulted on exactly ONE path. startDm() writes the saved name when a chat is opened from New Chat / Message Yourself — which is why the name corrected itself after opening — while every other path used server data, and refreshPeerIdentity() actively OVERWROTE a saved name with the registered one on its next background revalidation (once per TTL/session). Introduced peerDisplayName() (features/contacts/model), the single precedence rule: the name YOU saved wins over the name the peer registered; falls back to the registered name for someone not in your book or when the book has not loaded; returns undefined when neither side has a usable name so callers keep what they have; group rows are untouched (no peerId to look up). Applied at both the WRITE side (refreshPeerIdentity, both the TTL path and the profile-changed push, so a revalidation can no longer downgrade a saved name) and the READ side (toConversationRow for the chat list, useConversationIdentity for the chat header), the latter being what makes a saved name appear WITHOUT having to open the chat first. Exposed discoveredContacts() from the contacts barrel as a cache read (no re-discovery). Verified: full jest suite 502/502 pass (10 new tests), tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors and no boundary violation. Not re-tested on a device — no Android hardware attached to this machine.

bugs.title: Email-prompt bottom sheet reappears on every login even when an email is already saved
bugs.frequency: Every login
bugs.preconditions: An account that already has an email address linked/saved.
steps: Log in to an account that already has an email address associated with it.
Observe the email-prompt bottom sheet on the Home Screen.
bugs.expected: After logging in, the bottom sheet asking for an email should ONLY appear if the user has not added/linked an email. If the email is already present, the bottom sheet should not appear.
bugs.actual: The bottom sheet asking for email opens repeatedly after every login, regardless of whether the user already has an email saved.
bugs.user_impact: Users with an email already on file are repeatedly nagged for it on every login, a persistent, avoidable annoyance that looks like the app isn't remembering their profile.
bugs.suspected_cause: The bottom-sheet trigger likely checks a stale/cached email-presence flag instead of current profile state, or the check itself is missing.
bugs.notes: FIX (root-caused): the email is NOT a directory-profile field — profileShape.ts states it is a separately-verified identifier owned by the auth-service (GET /auth/account). useProfileGate decided purely from the LOCAL MMKV mirror, and purgeAccountData() wipes KVKeys.email on every sign-out, so immediately after any login the mirror is empty and the gate prompted unconditionally. useAccountInfo() does fetch the real email and mirror it, but it runs in parallel from AppTabs, so its answer always lost the race — and dismissal is session-only, which is why it returned every single login. The gate now asks the auth-service itself before deciding, via a new pure shouldPromptForProfile() (features/user/model/profileGate.ts): a mirrored email means never prompt; a server email means never prompt (and is re-mirrored so later launches short-circuit with no network); an UNANSWERED server (in flight or unreachable) means WAIT rather than prompt, which also removes the flash of the sheet before the answer lands. Only a definitive server no-email prompts. Verified: full jest suite 492/492 pass (5 new decision tests), tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors, no eslint-plugin-boundaries violation for the user→auth import (authApi depends only on infra, so no cycle). Not reproduced on a device — no Android hardware attached to this machine; fix is verified at the unit level against the exact reported condition.

testIds: authBootstrap.test.ts: cold start with a session already on the device
bugs.title: Cold start holds a splash screen on a network refresh — up to minutes before home appears
bugs.frequency: Every launch more than 15 minutes after the last one
bugs.preconditions: A signed-in install that has not been opened for more than 15 minutes, against a hibernating free-tier backend.
steps: Leave the app closed for more than 15 minutes so the access token expires and the Render services hibernate.
Open the app.
Time how long the splash screen stays up before the home screen appears.
bugs.expected: Home renders immediately from local data. The app is offline-first — §M0 rule 2 is that the UI never waits on the network on the render path.
bugs.actual: App.tsx renders <Splash/> until useAuthBootstrap reports ready, and the hook awaited a token refresh whenever the stored access token was expired. Against a hibernating free-tier backend that refresh alone takes 40-60s (client.ts documents a measured 44s wake, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT is 60s), and on timeout the hook then awaited TWO more network calls (requestChallenge, loginWithDeviceKey) before giving up — so the splash could hold for minutes.
bugs.user_impact: The app looks hung on every real launch. This is the first thing a user sees, so it reads as the whole app being broken rather than one slow request.
bugs.suspected_cause: The bootstrap conflated 'can we show the app' with 'is the access token fresh enough to open a socket'.
bugs.rootCause: Confirmed by reading the boot path and reproduced in a hook test: with the refresh mocked to never resolve, `ready` never became true.
bugs.notes: FIX: split the two questions the bootstrap had conflated — "can we show the app" and "is the access token fresh enough for a socket". If a session exists on the device at all (hasSession(), presence-only), the app now hydrates and reports ready IMMEDIATELY, whatever the token age; the chat list renders from the local DB, the HTTP client refreshes on its first 401, and the socket heals itself via 4001 -> refresh -> reconnect. VC-036 is not regressed: a fresh token is still wanted as early as possible so the first handshake is not doomed, so the refresh is still fired at once — it just runs BEHIND the app instead of in front of it. The no-session path (signed out but a device key survives) still attempts a silent restore, but is now bounded by MAX_SILENT_RESTORE_MS = 4000 so a hibernating backend cannot freeze the splash; a restore that lands later still navigates home on its own, because RootNavigator follows the auth store (state === active). Verified: full jest suite 521/521 pass (5 new hook tests, two of which fail against the old code by hanging until waitFor times out), tsc --noEmit clean, eslint 0 errors. Measured on device: not yet — needs a launch on real hardware to confirm the wall-clock improvement.

testIds: failureScenarios.test.ts: a message dropped by fan-out
bugs.title: A message the device was pushed for never reaches the chat, and no reconnect ever heals it — the sender still sees blue read ticks
bugs.feature: Chat / messaging — inbound persistence + reconnect backfill
bugs.device: Pixel emulator (Android 16, x86_64) receiving; OPPO CPH2643 (Android 16) sending
bugs.frequency: Intermittent — 2 confirmed occurrences in a 45-minute two-device session
bugs.reproducibility: Intermittent. Reproduced once deliberately (recipient process killed with `am kill`, sender sends, push wakes the process); a second identical attempt persisted correctly.
bugs.preconditions: Two signed-in devices in the same DM. Recipient's app process is not running (killed by the OS or by the user), so the inbound message arrives via an FCM wake rather than the live WebSocket.
steps: Device A and device B are signed in to the same DM.
Kill B's app PROCESS without force-stopping the package: adb -s <B> shell am kill com.velchat (confirm with `pidof com.velchat` returning empty).
From A, send a message (test used the text 'KILL2').
On B, confirm the push arrived: adb -s <B> shell dumpsys notification --noredact | grep android.text  ->  shows 'KILL2'.
Open VelChat on B from the launcher and open that DM.
Scroll the whole thread. Cold-start B several times and reopen the thread.
bugs.expected: A message the device was woken for is persisted to the local DB by the wake, or — failing that — pulled in by the next `sync {cursor}` + `?afterSeq=` backfill on reconnect (§L6). The recipient must end up holding every message the sender sees, and a read receipt must only ever be sent for a message that was actually stored.
bugs.actual: KILL2 produced a notification on B (proved by dumpsys) but never appeared in B's conversation. It is still absent after 3 app cold starts and multiple reconnects, i.e. the loss is permanent, not a render delay. Meanwhile A shows KILL2 with BLUE double ticks (read). The same signature was seen earlier in the session for two messages ('G' and 'M', 08:59) that A shows as read and B has never held.
bugs.user_impact: Silent, permanent message loss with a POSITIVE read confirmation to the sender. This is the worst failure a messenger can have: the sender believes the recipient read it, the recipient never saw it, and nothing in either UI indicates anything went wrong. No user action can recover the message.
bugs.suspected_cause: Two candidates, not yet separated: (a) the headless push wake posts the notification but its DB write is lost when the process is reaped before the WatermelonDB write commits; (b) the message is never durably fanned out (see VC-001) and the reconnect backfill does not re-request it. Either way the CLIENT-side defect is the same: the `sync {cursor}` + `afterSeq` backfill is not self-healing — a gap that exists once stays forever. The false `read` receipt means a receipt is being emitted from a path that does not require the message row to exist locally.
bugs.notes:
Evidence: scratchpad/shots/a_inline_rx.png (A shows KILL2 09:39 with blue ticks) vs scratchpad/shots/b_kill2_check.png (B's thread jumps BG1 09:37 -> KILL1 09:37 -> hhh 09:40, no KILL2). Related backend defect VC-001 may be the upstream cause, but the client must still heal the gap on reconnect and must not report `read` for a message it does not hold.

FIX (frontend): pageBackfill/backfillConversation take an optional `fromSeq`, and the gap probe passes the pre-apply `localMax` — so the repair asks the server from the LOWER edge of the hole instead of from the message that revealed it. Re-fetching the rows already held between localMax and the incoming seq is free: applyServerMessages dedups on (conversation_id, seq) and on client_msg_id inside the write lock. Three end-to-end tests added to failureScenarios.test.ts, driving the real engine against the fake server, written RED first — and rewritten once when the first version passed for the wrong reason (bootConnected’s own reconnect backfill was healing the hole), so each test now brings the socket up while the device is already caught up. Verified: 537/537 jest, tsc clean, eslint 0 errors.

STILL OPEN, tracked separately: (a) the FALSE READ TICK is not this fix — markConversationRead and read-on-arrival emit a CUMULATIVE read watermark at the local MAX, which covers a missing seq beneath it; clamping every read/delivered watermark to the highest CONTIGUOUS seq actually held is the correct fix and is filed as its own bug because it changes tick semantics everywhere and needs its own tests. (b) a hole detected once is only remembered in memory (gapProbedFrom), so a hole that a probe fails to close is forgotten on restart — persisting unhealed holes for retry is follow-up work. (c) VelChatMessagingService could enqueue a durable `resync` marker when JS is dead, the same fallback its siblings already have. (d) If the backend never durably stored or re-serves the message, no client change recovers it (see VC-001) — the fix then converts silent loss into an honest grey tick rather than a recovery.
bugs.rootCause: CONFIRMED by tracing the whole path. THREE facts compose into permanent loss. (1) A data push delivered to a DEAD process is handled entirely in Kotlin — VelChatMessagingService.handleMessage posts the notification and acks "delivered", then calls PushBridge.emit whose return value is discarded; PushBridge.liveContext() returns null when there is no JS to emit to and, unlike onNewToken/onDeletedMessages, there is NO store.enqueueEvent fallback. So the wake never writes the message to WatermelonDB and leaves no durable record that anything was missed. The only remaining route to the DB is a later REST backfill. (2) Every backfill cursor in the client is MAX(seq) — SyncEngine.pageBackfill, backfillInbox, and the content-fill and load-older paths all derive from maxSeqForConversation/minSeqForConversation — so once ANY newer message lands, the missing seq sits below the cursor and no afterSeq request can ever reach it again. (3) onInboundMessage already did the hard part: it reads localMax BEFORE applying, and shouldProbeGap correctly proves a hole exists — then it called backfillConversation, which re-reads MAX *after* applyServerMessage has moved it up to the revealing seq, so it fetched from ABOVE the hole and repaired nothing. The precisely-correct lower edge was captured, used for the predicate and the loop-guard memo, and then thrown away instead of being used as the fetch cursor.

bugs.title: Chat thread does not follow the newest message — incoming and own-sent bubbles land hidden behind the composer
bugs.feature: Chat / messaging — message list scroll behaviour
bugs.device: Reproduced on BOTH the OPPO CPH2643 (Android 16) and the Pixel emulator (Android 16)
bugs.frequency: Intermittent but very common — hit on the majority of message arrivals in a 45-minute session
bugs.reproducibility: Reproduced repeatedly on both devices, for incoming messages, for the user's own sent messages, and after opening the chat from a notification.
bugs.preconditions: A DM with enough history to be scrollable (the thread used had ~40 messages). The list is already at the bottom, showing the newest message.
steps: Open a DM and make sure the newest message is visible at the bottom (tap the jump-to-latest button if it is showing).
Have the peer send a message — or type and send one yourself.
Watch the bottom of the thread.
bugs.expected: The thread follows the newest message: the new bubble scrolls into view above the composer, the way WhatsApp does. This is what `shouldScrollToLatest` + `scrollToOffset({offset: 0})` in ChatScreen were added to guarantee.
bugs.actual: The list stays anchored on the OLD content. The new bubble is left below the fold — typically clipped behind the composer, so only a sliver of it shows — and after two or three arrivals the jump-to-latest button appears and the user has to scroll by hand. The offset ends up wrong by almost exactly the height of the newly inserted bubbles.
bugs.user_impact: The single most-used interaction in the app feels broken. A user sends a message and cannot see it; a message arrives and they do not know. Reported directly by the product owner as 'new message ane ya krne pe chup jata hai, scroll krke upar krna pdta hai'.
bugs.suspected_cause: CONFIRMED by reading @shopify/flash-list@2.3.2: `maintainVisibleContentPosition` is ENABLED BY DEFAULT (RecyclerView.js -> maintainVisibleContentPositionInternal sets `minIndexForVisible: 0` whenever `maintainVisibleContentPosition?.disabled` is not true). The chat list is `inverted`, which FlashList implements purely as a scaleY(-1) transform, so a NEW message is inserted at internal index 0 — the scroll START. The native anchor therefore pins the viewport and pushes the scroll offset out by the inserted height, undoing the `scrollToOffset({offset: 0})` the follow effect issues in the same commit. The library's own follow knob does not help: `autoscrollToBottomThreshold` defaults to -1 (disabled) and targets the internal END (the OLDEST messages in an inverted list), and `autoscrollToTopThreshold` is declared in FlashListProps.d.ts but is NEVER READ anywhere in the 2.3.2 implementation.
bugs.notes:
Evidence: scratchpad/shots/b_fg_follow.png (B at the bottom, F1-F3 arrive, list stays on S8 and the jump FAB appears), scratchpad/shots/b_one.png (single message ONE1 arrives, list left exactly one bubble short), scratchpad/shots/a_own_follow.png (A's OWN sent ONE1 clipped behind the composer), scratchpad/shots/b_offline_send.png (own offline sends clipped). The race explains the intermittency: sometimes the manual scroll lands after the anchor adjustment and it looks fine.

FIX: the follow now goes through FlashList's `scrollToIndex({index:0})` instead of `scrollToOffset({offset:0})`, fired from `onContentSizeChange` rather than the data effect. Root cause confirmed by reading useRecyclerViewController.js: on every data change FlashList measures how far the FIRST VISIBLE item moved and calls scrollAnchorRef.scrollBy(diff) to cancel the shift, gated on a `pauseOffsetCorrection` ref that ONLY scrollToIndex raises — so a plain offset scroll was undone every time and the thread landed exactly one bubble short. Firing from onContentSizeChange means index 0 has a real layout instead of the stale one it would have in the same commit. Anchoring is deliberately kept: it is the right behaviour for a reader scrolled up in history, whom shouldScrollToLatest still leaves alone; a drag cancels any pending follow so loadOlder growing the content is never mistaken for a new message. An intermediate attempt using scrollToOffset from onContentSizeChange plus a requestAnimationFrame retry was built and tested on device and still landed one bubble short — that is what identified the pauseOffsetCorrection gate. VERIFIED ON DEVICE: a four-message burst now ends with the newest message fully visible above the composer (scratchpad/shots/v2_own_follow.png) where the same burst on the previous build left it clipped (v_own_follow.png). Still to verify with a second device: the INCOMING-message path, and the notification tap-through landing position.

REGRESSED AND RE-FIXED, properly this time. The scroll-command approach was wrong in kind, not in detail: three versions were tried (scrollToOffset, scrollToOffset plus a frame, scrollToIndex plus a 180ms retry) and all three lost the same race, because FlashList re-pins the viewport through an invisible ScrollAnchor and that is a STATE update landing a render or two after any callback we can scroll from. The newest bubble kept ending up one message below the fold, intermittently — and it came back on the product owner reproducing it with the keyboard up. FINAL FIX: the list uses the library own chat pattern. Not inverted, rows reversed into ascending order at the list (never in the query, so every grouping flag stays attached to its own row and the rendered result is identical to what the inverted list drew), maintainVisibleContentPosition.autoscrollToBottomThreshold pins the end, startRenderingFromBottom opens on the newest, and loadOlder moves from onEndReached to onStartReached. There is no scroll command left to lose a race. shouldScrollToLatest is gone; autoScroll.ts now only measures distance-from-bottom for the jump button. VERIFIED ON THE REAL DEVICE with the keyboard up, the exact case that was failing: five messages sent, the newest fully visible above the composer, no jump button.

Pull down the shade and tap the notification body (not an action).
Look at the chat header.

bugs.title: Notification group summary says "N new messages" but N is the number of chats, not the number of messages
bugs.frequency: Every time two or more conversations have notifications
bugs.preconditions: At least two conversations holding undismissed message notifications, so the group summary is posted at all.
steps: With VelChat backgrounded and notifications from more than one chat pending, have a peer send 8 messages in one conversation.
Read the summary: adb shell dumpsys notification --noredact | grep -A2 GROUP_SUMMARY
Repeat with exactly ONE new message arriving.

bugs.title: Notification message lines are ordered by arrival, not by message time — an out-of-order push shows the wrong 'latest' message
bugs.frequency: Whenever FCM delivers two messages out of order — not rare, FCM gives no ordering guarantee
bugs.reproducibility: Reproduced once by holding one push back (recipient package force-stopped) and letting a later one land first.
bugs.preconditions: Two messages for the same conversation where the second-sent one is delivered to the device first.
steps: Send message 1 while the recipient package is in the stopped state, so FCM holds it.
Launch the recipient app (clearing FLAG_STOPPED) and send message 2 — FCM releases the held message 1 after message 2 lands.
Expand the notification and read the message lines.
bugs.expected: The MessagingStyle thread is ordered by the message's own time / seq, so the last line is the newest message — matching what the chat itself shows.
bugs.actual: The thread listed '... BG1, KILL2, KILL1' — KILL1 (09:37) below KILL2 (09:39) — and the collapsed notification therefore advertised KILL1 as the latest message. The in-app conversation ordered the same two messages correctly, so this is purely the notification's own line store.
bugs.user_impact: The notification tells the user the wrong thing is the most recent message, and the preview they glance at on the lock screen can be a message they have already seen.
bugs.suspected_cause: Lines are appended to the per-conversation store in arrival order and rendered in that order. The push payload already carries `seq`, which the reply/mark-read actions use — sorting the stored lines by it before building MessagingStyle would make the order independent of FCM's (explicitly unguaranteed) delivery order.
bugs.notes:
Evidence: scratchpad/shots/b_reply_open.png (expanded notification shows S6, S7, S8, BG1, KILL2, KILL1) vs scratchpad/shots/a_inline_rx.png (chat shows KILL1 09:37 then KILL2 09:39, correct).

FIX: `PushStore.Line` now carries the message's own `seq`, persisted as the JSON key `"q"`, and `showMessage` passes the push's seq into `appendLine`. `appendLine` SORTS before applying the `MAX_LINES` cap, and that order is the fix rather than a detail: capping first dropped whichever line FCM happened to deliver earliest, so an out-of-order push could evict a message newer than the one it kept. `setContentText` and `setLargeIcon` now read the newest INCOMING line (`lines.lastOrNull { !it.mine }`) instead of the message that arrived last, so the collapsed row and the face on it agree with the expanded thread — incoming only, because an inline reply can sort last and quoting the user's own words back at them is not a notification about anything.

MIGRATION for installs whose stored lines predate `q`: in `sortBySeq` each entry inherits the rank of the one before it and the sort is stable, so a legacy thread ranks entirely at zero and comes back exactly as stored — the only order anyone ever knew for it — while an inline reply (also seq 0) ranks immediately after the message it answered.

KNOWN LIMITATION, left open deliberately: `Line.at` is still the ARRIVAL timestamp (`System.currentTimeMillis()` at `showMessage`), because the push payload carries no message timestamp. MessagingStyle stamps each line with it, so a REORDERED thread can show non-monotonic times until the backend sends a message timestamp. The order is now right; the clock beside it is not.

NO AUTOMATED TEST: this project has no Kotlin test source set at all — `android/app/src` holds only `main`, `dev` and `prod` — so nothing in the push package is reachable from Jest. Verified by code review against the report; the live repro still needs re-running on a device.

LIVE RE-TEST 2026-09-19 on the two-device setup, following this entry's own steps (recipient package force-stopped so FCM holds a message, app launched to clear FLAG_STOPPED, a second message sent into the release window). RESULT: the expanded thread came back in seq order with the newest line last (OK4, FIN1, FIN2, FIN3, FIN4, ORD2) and the collapsed row quoted the newest, where the pre-fix run of the same procedure had produced KILL2 above KILL1. Both messages also landed in the conversation in the right order with nothing lost. CAVEAT recorded honestly: FCM released the held message quickly enough that a strictly OUT-OF-ORDER delivery was not forced on this run, so what this proves is correct ordering and no regression, not the reordering path itself firing. That path is covered by code review only (there is no Kotlin test source set in this project).

bugs.title: Notification re-lists messages the user has already read once the chat is reopened and a new message arrives
bugs.feature: Notifications — thread clearing on chat open
bugs.frequency: Every time a chat is opened from its own notification and a later message then arrives
bugs.preconditions: A conversation whose notification the user has already opened and read.
steps: Receive several messages while backgrounded (test used S1..S8) so the notification thread holds them.
Tap the notification to open the chat and read them; the tray entry disappears.
Background the app again and have the peer send ONE new message.
Expand the new notification.
bugs.expected: The thread starts fresh from the new message. PushNotifications.cancel() already calls store.clearLines(conversationId) precisely for this, and its comment says so: 'opening a chat and then receiving one new message would rebuild the notification with every line the user had already read.'
bugs.actual: The rebuilt notification listed S6, S7, S8, BG1 and then the new lines — messages the user had already read in the app minutes earlier.
bugs.user_impact: The user is re-notified about messages they have already read, so the notification badge and preview overstate what is actually new and the thread is cluttered with stale content. It also undermines trust that opening a chat actually clears it.
bugs.suspected_cause: The chat-open path does not reach `PushNotifications.cancel()`. The tray entry vanishing on tap is explained by the notification's own AUTO_CANCEL flag, which removes the posted notification but does NOT run the app's clearing code, so `store.clearLines()` never executes and the stored lines survive to be rebuilt into the next notification. Needs a check that `setActiveConversationForPush`/`clearConversationNotification` fires on chat mount and that it routes into `cancel()` rather than only `NotificationManager.cancel()`.
bugs.notes:
Evidence: scratchpad/shots/b_shade.png (S3..S8 before opening), scratchpad/shots/b_tapthrough.png (chat opened, tray cleared, all read), scratchpad/shots/b_reply_open.png (next notification still carries S6, S7, S8, BG1).

ROOT CAUSE FOUND and FIXED via VC-062. The clearing path was wired correctly all along — clearConversationNotification -> VelChatPushModule.clearConversation -> PushNotifications.cancel -> store.clearLines — but it only ran from the chat screen's MOUNT effect. A notification tap RESUMES an already-mounted ChatScreen, so that effect never re-ran, and the tray entry disappearing was just the notification's own AUTO_CANCEL flag removing the posted notification while the stored lines and counters survived. useMessages now also clears on every return to the foreground. Live re-verification pending a second device.

LIVE VERIFIED 2026-09-19: after opening the chat and backgrounding again, the next notification carried only the new messages — no line from the batch the user had already read.

bugs.title: Chat-list preview can regress to an older message — the preview is written unconditionally while the timestamp is guarded
bugs.frequency: Whenever messages are applied out of order (out-of-order push, or a backfill landing after a live message)
bugs.reproducibility: Observed once live; the code path is deterministic once an older patch arrives after a newer one.
bugs.preconditions: Two messages for one conversation applied in the wrong order.
steps: Arrange for message 2 (newer) to be applied to the local DB before message 1 (older) — e.g. an FCM-held push released after a later one.
Open the Chats list and read that row's preview and timestamp.
bugs.expected: The row previews the newest message. A stale patch must not be able to move the preview backwards, exactly as it cannot move the sort key backwards.
bugs.actual: The row previewed 'KILL1' while 'KILL2' was the newer message, and stayed that way until a still-newer message arrived.
bugs.user_impact: The chat list — the app's home screen — shows the wrong 'last message' for a conversation, so the user's summary of their inbox is wrong and can point at a message they have already read.
bugs.suspected_cause: CONFIRMED in code. In `upsertConversation` the sort key is protected: `if (patch.lastMessageAt !== undefined && patch.lastMessageAt >= (c.lastMessageAt ?? 0)) c.lastMessageAt = patch.lastMessageAt;` with the comment 'Never move the sort key backwards (a stale patch mustn't reorder the list)'. The preview immediately above it has no such guard: `if (patch.lastMessagePreview !== undefined) c.lastMessagePreview = patch.lastMessagePreview;`. So a stale patch is prevented from reordering the list but is still allowed to overwrite what the row says.
bugs.notes:
Evidence: scratchpad/shots/b_after_reply.png (row reads 'KILL1' while KILL2 was newer). Fix is to move the preview write inside the same freshness check as the timestamp.

FIX: the preview write now sits behind the same freshness check as the sort key in upsertConversation — a single `fresher` predicate gates both, so a stale patch can no longer overwrite what the row says while being correctly refused a reorder.

bugs.title: Composer's emoji, attach, camera and mic buttons are dead controls that look and behave as if they work
bugs.frequency: Every time
bugs.preconditions: Any open chat.
steps: Open any chat.
Tap the smiley, the paperclip, the camera, and (with the field empty) the round mic button.
bugs.expected: A control the user can press either does something or is visibly unavailable. Four of the five controls on the primary input surface should not be indistinguishable from working ones.
bugs.actual: All four are wired to `noop`. They render at full opacity, carry `accessibilityRole="button"` with a real label, and give press feedback (opacity dips to 0.6, and the mic shares the send button's full brand fill), so nothing tells the user they are inert. Tapping does nothing at all — no sheet, no toast, no disabled state.

bugs.notes:
Minimum viable fix for a release build: hide the unimplemented controls, or render them disabled (reduced opacity + accessibilityState disabled) so neither sighted nor screen-reader users are misled.

FIX: `PillIconButton` lost its `onPress` prop entirely — emoji, attach and camera now render a `Pressable` with a real `disabled` and `accessibilityState={{disabled: true}}`, and the pressed-opacity branch is gone, so a tap produces no fake response at all and TalkBack announces them as disabled rather than as working buttons. The primary circle does the same conditionally (`disabled={!hasText}`, `accessibilityState` following it, and `opacity: pressed && hasText ? 0.8 : 1`), so the one control that is a send button half the time and an unbuilt mic the other half reports which one it currently is.

Everything visual is UNCHANGED on purpose: the icons, the 34x38 box and the full opacity are exactly what shipped. `composerControls.test.tsx` (7 tests) pins that box and the opacity so a well-meant "just dim them" is caught as the visual change it would be.

STILL ACTIONABLE — PRODUCT DECISION OUTSTANDING. What shipped only stops these controls lying about being enabled. Whether an unbuilt control should be HIDDEN or visibly greyed has NOT been decided, and this fix deliberately does neither. Marked Fixed for the a11y/misleading-affordance defect as reported; the visual treatment is a separate call the product owner still owes.

bugs.title: A 48dp empty band sits between the composer and the keyboard whenever the keyboard is open
bugs.frequency: Every time the keyboard opens in a chat
bugs.preconditions: Any open chat.
steps: Open a chat and tap the message field so the keyboard comes up.
Look at the gap between the bottom of the composer pill and the top of the keyboard.
bugs.expected: The composer sits close above the keyboard, the way WhatsApp and every other messenger do — a few dp at most.
bugs.actual: `paddingBottom` is `t.spacing.huge` (48dp) when the keyboard is up, leaving a wide empty strip between the input bar and the keyboard. On a 2412px screen this is roughly 144px of dead space that could be showing another message.
bugs.user_impact: With the keyboard open — the state the user is in while actually writing — the app shows one fewer message than it needs to and the input bar looks detached from the keyboard. It reads as a layout mistake rather than a design choice.
bugs.suspected_cause: The keyboard-up branch was tuned while the manual keyboard-height lift was being worked out and the compensation was left larger than it needs to be.
bugs.notes:
Evidence: scratchpad/shots/a_cal.png and a_own_follow.png — the white band between the composer pill and the keyboard's suggestion strip. Same file also sets `borderTopWidth: 0` alongside a `borderTopColor`, so the intended separator between the thread and the composer never draws.

FIX: keyboard-up paddingBottom drops from spacing.huge (48dp) to spacing.xs (8dp), and borderTopWidth goes from 0 to 1 so the separator the style always declared actually draws. VERIFIED ON DEVICE: scratchpad/shots/v2_own_follow.png shows the hairline above the composer and the composer sitting close to the keyboard.

CORRECTION after on-device testing. Only HALF of this was a defect. The borderTopWidth 0 -> 1 fix is right and shipped: the separator the style always declared now draws. The 48dp padding is NOT over-generous, it is LOAD-BEARING — the parent lifts the bar by keyboardDidShow.endCoordinates.height, and under RN 0.86 Android edge-to-edge that value lands short of the keyboard the user actually sees. Trimming it to 8dp moved the input 40dp down and put it BEHIND the keyboard on a 3-button-nav CPH2643; caught on the device and reverted before it could ship. The white band is cosmetic and invisible against a light keyboard. The real fix is to correct the LIFT, not the padding, and that is separate work.

bugs.title: A chat left open while the app is backgrounded keeps marking arriving messages read — the sender gets a blue tick for a message nobody has seen
bugs.frequency: Every message that arrives while the app is backgrounded on a chat screen — i.e. constantly in normal use
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic once the state is set up; confirmed by reading the code path.
bugs.preconditions: The recipient has a conversation OPEN and then leaves the app or locks the screen. The chat screen stays mounted, because backgrounding does not unmount it.
steps: On device B open a DM and leave it open.
Press Home, or lock the screen. Do not go back to the chat list.
From device A send a message.
Look at the tick state on A.
bugs.expected: A message is only 'read' once the recipient can actually see it. A backgrounded app is showing nothing, so the ticks stay grey until the user returns to the chat — which is exactly the rule the push layer beside this already follows.
bugs.actual: The sender's bubble goes blue immediately. The SyncEngine reads every message landing in `activeConversationId` on arrival, and `useMessages` only ever cleared that id on UNMOUNT.
bugs.user_impact: Read receipts stop meaning anything: a sender is told their message was read by someone whose phone was in their pocket. It also silently clears the recipient's unread badge for messages they have never seen, so those messages can be lost in the list. This is very likely the read-receipt half of VC-051, where the sender saw blue ticks for a message the recipient never received at all.

The AppState listener in the same effect correctly does `setActiveConversationForPush(state === 'active' ? conversationId : null)` — it simply never does the equivalent for the engine, so the engine's idea of 'on screen' survives backgrounding.

Verified: 534/534 jest, tsc clean, eslint 0 errors. Live two-device re-verification still pending — the test phone was disconnected before it could be run.

testIds: failureScenarios.test.ts: a realtime frame with no body
bugs.title: A message whose realtime frame carries no body renders a permanently blank bubble — the REST recovery is dead code and the list would not re-render anyway
bugs.frequency: Every inbound message whose fan-out frame has no body
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic by code inspection; not yet reproduced live because today's plaintext messages happen to carry `text` on the wire.
bugs.preconditions: A peer sends a message the gateway relays WITHOUT a body — per docs/backend-integration-reference.md §4 the WS payload carries an optional `text`, so media and (at the E2EE phase) every message arrive metadata-only.
steps: Have a peer send a message the gateway relays with no `text` field while the chat is open.
Watch the bubble that appears.
Leave the chat and come back.
bugs.expected: The bubble shows the message. SyncEngine already tries: `if (m.content === undefined || m.content === '') { const filled = await fetchMessagesAfter(conv, m.seq - 1); await applyServerMessages(filled); }`.
bugs.actual: An empty bubble with only a timestamp, and an empty preview on the chat list. The recovery cannot work, for two independent reasons, and both must be fixed or the bubble stays blank.
bugs.user_impact: A received message shows as blank. The user has no idea what was said and no way to recover it inside the app. At the E2EE phase this would be every single inbound message.
bugs.suspected_cause: (a) THE FILL IS SKIPPED AS A DUPLICATE. `fetchMessagesAfter(conv, seq-1)` returns the same message, and `reconcileDecision` (syncLogic.ts:20-22) is `if (hasClientMsgIdRow) return 'update'; if (hasSeqRow) return 'skip';`. `hasSeqRow` is true — the row was inserted milliseconds earlier by the `applyServerMessage` on the line above. `hasClientMsgIdRow` can never be true for a peer's message: there is no client_msg_id on the wire, so the insert synthesises `srv_<conversationId>_<seq>` while the REST row carries the sender's real id. The decision is always 'skip', so content_plain is never written and the whole block is dead code for exactly the case its comment names. Every later catch-up funnels through the same decision, so the comment 'content syncs on next catch-up' is also untrue. (b) EVEN IF (a) IS FIXED, NOTHING RE-RENDERS. `observeMessages` is `.observeWithColumns(['state'])`, and WatermelonDB only emits when the matched-record SET changes or a NAMED column changes — a content_plain-only update on an already-matched row emits nothing.
bugs.notes:
Found by a code-level audit after the live session. Fix needs both halves: let the fill update a row matched by seq (e.g. treat a seq row with empty content as 'update'), and name `content_plain` in observeMessages' column list.

FIX, both halves — either alone still leaves a blank bubble.

(a) THE FILL CAN NOW LAND. `reconcileDecision` takes a new `seqRowMissingBody` input: a seq row we already hold WITHOUT a body reconciles as `update` instead of `skip`. It stays narrow on purpose — only a MISSING body earns a write, so an ordinary duplicate is still free, and a message that legitimately has no text (an attachment with no caption) offers none either and still skips. `applyServerMessages` computes it as `offersBody && bySeq.length > 0 && bySeq.every(r => !hasBody(r.contentPlain))`, resolves the update target as `byClient[0] ?? bySeq[0]` (a peer's message can never take the `client_msg_id` branch — there is none on the wire and the insert synthesises `srv_<conv>_<seq>`), and re-bumps the chat-list preview the bodiless frame had written as empty. The bump passes `byClient.length > 0 || own` rather than a flat `true`, so a refill corrects the preview without being counted as a second unread arrival.

(b) THE LIST NOW RE-RENDERS. `observeMessages` names `content_plain` in a new exported `MESSAGE_OBSERVED_COLUMNS`, kept beside the subscription so the two cannot drift. `observeWithColumns` emits only for the columns it is NAMED (or a change in the matched-record set), so before this the refill wrote the text into the database and nothing woke: the message was there, the text was there, and the user kept the empty bubble until they left the chat and came back.

The column test asserts the LIST rather than an emission, and that is deliberate: WatermelonDB observables do not emit under the Loki adapter Jest uses, so an emission-based test would fail identically whether the bug is present or not and would prove nothing.
