bugs.title: Opening a chat from a notification while another chat is on screen keeps the unsent draft — one tap can send it to the wrong person
bugs.feature: Chat / messaging — notification deep link into a live screen
bugs.component: apps/mobile/src/features/chat/ui/ChatScreen.tsx (local useState) + navigation/RootNavigator.tsx (no getId on the Chat screen)
bugs.frequency: Every notification tap taken while a different chat is already open
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic by code inspection — the same param-update path that VC-053 was filed and fixed on.
bugs.preconditions: The user is on a chat screen with unsent text in the composer, and taps a notification for a DIFFERENT conversation.
steps: Open the chat with contact A and type a message WITHOUT sending it.
Lock the phone or switch apps, leaving the chat screen mounted.
Receive a message from contact B and tap its notification.
Look at the composer, then press send.
bugs.expected: Opening a different conversation starts with an empty composer. A draft belongs to the chat it was written in.
bugs.actual: The screen is REUSED, not remounted: the deep link dispatches a NAVIGATE to `Chat`, and with no `getId` configured on the Chat screen the stack router reuses the current route's key and only swaps `route.params`. `useMessages`, `useConversationIdentity` and `useChatHeaderPresence` all re-run on the new conversationId, but every `useState` in ChatScreen survives — so the composer still holds A's text while `send` is now bound to B. One tap sends A's private message to B.
bugs.user_impact: A private message can be delivered to the wrong person with a single tap and no warning. That is a confidentiality failure, not just a UX slip. Lesser symptoms from the same cause: the first keystroke after the switch emits a typing signal to B while the field shows A's words; `offsetRef` carries over, so if the user had scrolled up in A's chat the auto-follow is silently disabled in B's until they scroll once; the jump-to-latest button can appear for a chat already at the bottom.
bugs.suspected_cause: ChatScreen holds `text`, `offsetRef`, `showJump`/`showJumpRef` and `newestIdRef` in component state and nothing resets them when `conversationId` changes. Fix: either give the Chat screen a `getId: ({ params }) => params.conversationId` so the deep link remounts it, or reset every piece of local state in an effect keyed on conversationId.
bugs.notes:
Found by a code-level audit. VC-053 fixed the TITLE on this exact entry point, which confirms the param-update path is real and exercised; the state carry-over was not addressed then.

FIX — and NOT the `getId` this entry proposed. `navigation/RootNavigator.tsx` is UNCHANGED: the Chat screen still has no `getId`, and the deep link still reuses the route and swaps `route.params`. What changed is entirely in `ChatScreen.tsx`: it is now a shell that reads `route.params` and renders the real screen — the old body, renamed `ChatThread` — as `<ChatThread key={conversationId} … />`. The key IS the reset. React tears the old thread down and builds a new one, so `text`, `offsetRef`, `showJump`/`showJumpRef` and `newestIdRef` cannot cross over, and whatever state `ChatThread` grows later is covered by construction instead of by somebody remembering to add it to a reset effect.

`getId` was considered and rejected for two reasons recorded in the file's doc comment. It remounts by PUSHING a second Chat route (StackRouter reuses a route only when the id matches) and native-stack keeps every route beneath the top mounted — so one live thread per notification tap, each holding a DB subscription and a FlashList, on the 3 GB reference device (§R5). And the route popped back to would sit on screen with NO active conversation, because the effect that claims it keys on the id rather than on focus and so never re-runs — re-opening VC-062. Remounting inside the route leaves the stack exactly as it is.

Covered by `conversationSwitch.test.tsx` (5 tests): the draft does not carry over, the previous chat's words cannot be sent to the new peer, the new conversation lands at the bottom rather than where the old one was left, the header still gets the conversation it was sent, and — the guard against over-correcting — an ordinary re-render that is NOT a conversation switch leaves a half-typed message alone.

testIds: presenceLifecycle.test.ts: a chat closed while its presence is still resolving
bugs.title: Backing out of a chat mid-resolve strands a 20s presence timer, and can permanently disable the only code that clears it
bugs.frequency: Whenever a chat is closed before its presence resolve finishes — a sub-second window, hit often on a slow network or a busy DB
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic by code inspection; needs the chat closed inside the await window.
bugs.preconditions: Open a chat and leave it again before the presence lookup completes.
steps: Open a chat and press back within roughly 300 ms, i.e. before the GET /presence round trip resolves.
Stay out of every chat.
Watch for JS-thread wakeups, or instrument startPeerPresencePolling.
bugs.expected: Leaving a chat releases everything it started. Per M7: every timer, listener, socket, subscription and worker is owned and disposable.
bugs.actual: activatePresence registers its map entry and starts its interval AFTER two awaits, and no cancellation token reaches it. The screen cleanup runs deactivatePresence first, so the map is empty and clearPeerPresenceTimer has nothing to clear; the promise then resumes and starts a 20 s setInterval for a chat that is closed. Its own guard makes every tick a no-op, so it is an invisible timer waking the JS thread every 20 s until the next chat is opened, a background suspend, or engine stop — and when push is unavailable scheduleSuspend returns early, so it ticks all night. Worse, if the back happens during the SHORTER await (a WatermelonDB find, which blocks behind any in-flight write such as an inbound message batch), deactivatePresence deletes nothing and the entry is written afterwards: activePresencePeers then holds a permanent ghost, its size can never reach 0 again, and clearPeerPresenceTimer inside deactivatePresence becomes dead code for the rest of the session. From then on, closing ANY chat stops clearing its presence poll.
bugs.user_impact: Battery and wakeups on the 3 GB reference device, exactly what the overnight-background contract M13 forbids. Silent, and a later chat open masks it because startPeerPresencePolling clears the timer first — which is why live testing never catches it.
bugs.suspected_cause: State is registered after awaits with no cancellation. Fix: capture a generation token before the first await and bail if deactivatePresence has run since, or register the map entry BEFORE the awaits so deactivate can always see it.
bugs.notes:
Found by a code-level audit after the live two-device session.

FIX: a `presenceEpoch` counter on the engine. `deactivatePresence` bumps it BEFORE the map delete — before, so an activate still awaiting sees the move rather than racing the delete — and the two paths that clear `activePresencePeers` wholesale, `stop()` and `onSessionCleared()`, bump it too. `activatePresence` captures the epoch before its first await and bails at three points: after the stored-peer lookup (`peerIdFor`), after the members fallback, and again after `refreshPeerPresence`.

The FIRST check is what kills the permanent ghost — everything past it writes to `activePresencePeers`, and it was that late write landing after the close's delete that made the map's size unable to reach 0 again and turned `clearPeerPresenceTimer` into dead code for the rest of the session. The LAST also undoes its own registration (`activePresencePeers.delete(conversationId)`, then `clearPeerPresenceTimer()` if it was the last chat), because by that point it has already registered and the network round trip is the widest window of the three.

Covered by `presenceLifecycle.test.ts`, written RED first and driving both windows with hand-resolved deferred promises so the race is deterministic rather than hoped for. Before the fix, `setInterval(fn, 20000)` was provably called for a chat that was already closed — the §M7/§M13 violation this entry describes, reproduced in a test rather than argued about.

bugs.title: PushStore's JSON blobs are read-modify-write across three threads — notification lines and counts can be lost or resurrected
bugs.component: apps/mobile/android/app/src/main/java/com/velchat/push/PushStore.kt (appendLine, clearLines, bumpCount, clearCount, setLastSeq, setMuted, setAvatars)
bugs.frequency: Whenever two of the three writer threads overlap — a push landing while a chat is opened or a notification dismissed
bugs.reproducibility: Race — rare per attempt, inevitable at scale.
bugs.preconditions: A push for one conversation arriving while the app clears another conversation's notification.
steps: Open chat B from its notification, so the RN native-modules thread runs clearLines for B.
In the same window, have a push for chat A arrive, so the FCM delivery thread runs appendLine for A.
Later, receive one new message in chat B and expand its notification.
bugs.expected: Each conversation's stored lines and counts are independent, and every update is durable.
bugs.actual: Each of the five maps — lines, counts, lastSeq, muted, avatars — is ONE SharedPreferences string holding every conversation, read whole and written back whole. Two threads that read before either writes will have the later write clobber the earlier. If the FCM thread wins, B's six lines survive its cancellation and the next message in B rebuilds the thread with every line the user already read — the VC-057 symptom, resurrected as a race rather than a missing call. If the other side wins, A's new line is lost and the notification shows only older lines for the message that just arrived. The same shape on counts either re-establishes a count the user just dismissed or drops a bump, and those counts feed the group summary total.
bugs.user_impact: Notifications intermittently re-show read messages, drop the message that just arrived, or report a total that matches nothing. Non-deterministic, so it reads to the user as the app being unreliable.
bugs.suspected_cause: The class doc claims every accessor is safe from any thread because SharedPreferences is internally synchronised. That is true for a single getString or putString and false for the read-then-write pairs used throughout. Three writers in one process: VelChatMessagingService on FCM's delivery thread, PushActionReceiver on the main thread, VelChatPushModule on the RN native-modules thread. Fix: one synchronized lock around every read-modify-write in the class; all callers share a single SharedPreferences instance in a single process, so that is sufficient.
bugs.notes:
Distinct from VC-033, which is about the pending-event queue. This is the other five maps. Found by a code-level audit after the live two-device session.

FIX: one `synchronized(WRITE_LOCK)` monitor wrapping every read-modify-write in the class — `appendLine`, `clearLines`, `clearAllLines`, `bumpCount`, `clearCount`, `clearAllCounts`, `setLastSeq`, `setMuted`, `putNames` (both name maps) and `putPersonAvatar`, plus `enqueueEvent`/`takeEvents` on the pending-event queue this entry split off from VC-033.

The monitor is on the COMPANION object, and that is load-bearing rather than a style choice: `PushStore(context)` is constructed FRESH at each entry point — the FCM service, the broadcast receiver, the RN module — so an instance monitor would have been three separate locks guarding one file, which is no lock at all. Android hands every instance the same `SharedPreferences` object for a given file in a given process, so one process-wide monitor is exactly the scope of the contention.

Deliberately OUTSIDE the lock: the blind `commit()` writes (`setCredentials`, `clearSession`, `setActiveConversation`) and the pure single reads. Those have nothing to read first, so there is no read-modify-write to protect, and `commit()` blocks on a disk sync — nothing here is worth holding a monitor across one. `clearAllCounts`/`clearAllLines` are blind too but still take it, because a `bumpCount` that read the map before them and writes after would otherwise put back a count the user just cleared.

The class doc is corrected in place: its claim that every accessor was thread-safe "because SharedPreferences is internally synchronised" is true of a single `getString`/`putString` and false of every pair this class actually uses, which is why the comment is now the explanation of the race instead of the reason nobody looked for it.

NO AUTOMATED TEST: this project has no Kotlin test source set at all — `android/app/src` holds only `main`, `dev` and `prod` — so nothing in the push package is reachable from Jest. Verified by code review against the report; the live repro still needs re-running on a device. A lost-update race across three native threads is not reachable from the JS test harness in any case.

bugs.title: Swiping a notification away clears its count but keeps its message lines, so dismissed messages reappear in the next notification
bugs.frequency: Every dismissed notification followed by a new message in the same chat
bugs.preconditions: A conversation whose notification the user swiped away without reading.
steps: Let three messages from one contact arrive while the app is backgrounded; the notification lists three lines.
Swipe the notification away without opening the chat.
Have that contact send one more message.
Expand the new notification.
bugs.expected: The new notification lists only the new message. Every other teardown path clears both halves — PushNotifications.cancel does clearCount AND clearLines, with a comment saying exactly why.
bugs.actual: The dismiss branch clears only the count and returns. The stored lines survive, so appendLine returns all four and the rebuilt MessagingStyle re-lists the three messages the user deliberately dismissed, while setNumber says 1.
bugs.user_impact: Dismissing a notification does not actually dismiss its contents. The user reads four new messages for one new arrival, and the dismissal gesture stops meaning anything.
bugs.suspected_cause: A separate receiver branch that the VC-057 fix did not reach; it needs the same clearLines the cancel path has. SECONDARY, same area: postSummary builds the group summary with setGroupSummary true and NO delete intent, unlike every per-conversation notification — so dismissing the bundle runs none of our clearing for the summary, and on any OEM build that does not deliver child delete intents on a group dismissal the counts survive wholesale and the next single message re-posts a summary counting messages already swept away.
bugs.notes:
Found by a code-level audit after the live two-device session. Deterministic, unlike the race in the sibling PushStore report.

FIX: the `ACTION_DISMISS` branch now calls `store.clearLines(conversationId)` alongside `clearCount`, matching `PushNotifications.cancel`, which has always dropped both halves.

The SECONDARY half of this report is fixed too, because a backstop that does half of what it backs up just relocates the bug to the group path. `postSummary` gained `setDeleteIntent(summaryDismissIntent(context))`, carrying a new `ACTION_DISMISS_SUMMARY` that `PushActionReceiver.onReceive` answers BEFORE the conversation-id extra is demanded — the summary belongs to no single conversation, so it carries no id and the existing `getStringExtra(...) ?: return` would have swallowed it silently. That branch clears counts AND lines wholesale (`clearAllCounts` + `clearAllLines`). It is idempotent on builds where the children's delete intents do arrive, and it is the only clearing that happens on the OEM builds where they do not.

NO AUTOMATED TEST: this project has no Kotlin test source set at all — `android/app/src` holds only `main`, `dev` and `prod` — so nothing in the push package is reachable from Jest. Verified by code review against the report; the live repro still needs re-running on a device.

LIVE VERIFIED 2026-09-19 following this entry's own steps: three messages arrived while backgrounded and were swiped away unread, then one more was sent. The rebuilt notification reported android.messages = Parcelable[] (1) — one line, not four. Pre-fix the same procedure re-listed every dismissed message.

testIds: chatOpenEffects.test.tsx: paging through history is not re-opening the chat
bugs.title: Every load-older page re-runs the open-the-chat side effects, briefly un-suppressing notifications for the chat on screen
bugs.frequency: Once per page of scrollback
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic for the wasted work; the notification window is a race inside it.
bugs.preconditions: A conversation with enough history to page through.
steps: Open a long chat and scroll up through several pages of history.
Watch the network: a receipts fetch and a read frame go out per page.
Have the peer send a message during the scrollback.
bugs.expected: Opening a chat is a one-time act. Growing the local window should only re-subscribe the message query.
bugs.actual: The effect is keyed on conversationId, meId and limit, but only observeMessages depends on limit. Each loadOlder therefore tears the effect down and re-runs ALL of it: a receipts GET, a read receipt frame, a clearConversation bridge call, and the pair setActiveConversationForPush(null) then setActiveConversationForPush(conversationId). Those two are async bridge calls, so for the length of one native round trip the native side believes NO chat is on screen — and a push landing in that window posts a heads-up notification for the chat the user is staring at, the exact failure the active-conversation mechanism exists to prevent. Ten pages of scrollback is ten such windows.
bugs.user_impact: Redundant network on every page of scrollback, and an occasional notification for the conversation that is currently open. The engine's own window is zero-width because setActiveConversation is synchronous; only the native mirror is exposed.
bugs.suspected_cause: One effect doing two jobs. Split it: keep the observeMessages subscription keyed on limit, and move the open-the-chat actions plus the AppState listener into an effect keyed on conversationId alone.
bugs.notes:
Found by a code-level audit after the live two-device session.

FIX: the `useMessages` effect was split in two, exactly as this entry proposed. The open-the-chat work — `clearUnread` plus the read frame, the receipts GET, `syncEngine.setActiveConversation`, `setActiveConversationForPush`, the `clearConversationNotification` bridge call and the AppState listener — now sits in an effect keyed on `conversationId` ALONE, with its teardown (`appStateSub.remove()` and both active-conversation withdrawals) moved across with it. A second effect keyed on `[conversationId, limit]` does the only thing a wider window actually changes: subscribe `observeMessages` and release the narrower subscription.

`meId` came out of both dependency arrays. Neither half ever read it — it is a stable account id — so keeping it there only ever meant more ways to re-run all of the above.

The consequence that matters: `loadOlder` no longer tears down and re-runs the `setActiveConversationForPush(null)` → `…(conversationId)` pair. That hop is an async bridge call, so each page of scrollback opened a window in which the native side believed NO chat was on screen and a push landing inside it posted a heads-up notification for the chat the user was reading.

Covered by `chatOpenEffects.test.tsx` (4 tests): a wider window re-subscribes and releases the old subscription; the open-the-chat side effects do NOT re-run per page; the push layer is never told that no chat is on screen while one is; and — the guard against over-correcting — a DIFFERENT conversation still re-opens, and unmount still lets go.

bugs.title: The read watermark is sent at the local MAX seq, so it covers messages the device does not hold — the sender gets a blue tick for a message that was never received
bugs.frequency: Every time a conversation has a hole in its seq range
bugs.reproducibility: Observed live twice, and confirmed deterministic by code inspection.
bugs.preconditions: The device is missing a message at some seq N while holding messages above it — e.g. after a fan-out drop, the exact condition VC-051 describes.
steps: Arrange for a message at seq N to be missing locally while N+1 and above are present (see VC-051 for the repro).
Open that conversation on the recipient device.
Look at the tick state for message N on the SENDER.
bugs.expected: A read receipt means the recipient saw the message. A device must never acknowledge a seq it does not hold.
bugs.actual: Receipts are cumulative watermarks — one frame carries upToSeq and covers every message at or below it — and every emitter derives that number from the local MAX seq, not the highest CONTIGUOUS seq. markConversationRead runs on every chat open and on the notification read and reply actions, and uses maxSeqForConversation; read-on-arrival uses the incoming seq itself, so the very frame that OPENS a hole immediately reports read up to its own seq; the backfill loop does the same with its highest page seq. A native path acknowledges read straight over REST from a process with no database open at all. Nothing anywhere checks that a row exists for the seq being acknowledged, and mergeWatermark is monotonic, so an over-advanced read is permanent for the life of the install.
bugs.user_impact: Read receipts stop meaning anything in exactly the situation where they matter most. A sender is told a message was read when the recipient never received it and never will — which is how the VC-051 message loss stayed invisible to both sides. It also clears the recipient's unread badge for messages they have never seen.
bugs.suspected_cause: CONFIRMED in code. Fix: replace the maxSeqForConversation used for RECEIPTS with a highest-contiguous-seq query (highest seq with no hole beneath it, relative to the conversation's known floor so that trimmed history and deleted messages are not mistaken for holes), and clamp the read-on-arrival seq to that value so the frame that opens a hole reports only up to the previous localMax. The same clamp applies to the delivered watermark fed from push. Deliberately NOT bundled with the VC-051 backfill fix: it changes tick semantics on every path and needs its own tests, and getting the floor wrong would under-report reads, which is a worse bug than the one being fixed.
bugs.notes:
Split out of VC-051 during that investigation. VC-062 (a backgrounded-but-mounted chat marking arrivals read) widened the window and is fixed; this is the independent, underlying defect.

FIX: a new `maxContiguousSeqForConversation` in `infra/db/messages.ts` — the highest seq with no KNOWN hole beneath it — over a bounded `CONTIGUITY_SCAN = 500` row scan (`seq > 0`, seq DESC, then sorted ascending).

"Known" is the load-bearing word, and the two design choices under it are the two ways this fix could have been worse than the bug. It starts from the OLDEST row held rather than from seq 1, because the device keeps a bounded window and a conversation whose oldest local row is seq 900 is normal, not a gap — reading it as one would pin every receipt at 0 and leave every sender on a single grey tick forever. And it walks UP from there so it stops at the LOWEST hole; stopping at the highest would still acknowledge every deeper one. A deleted message still counts as held, because a tombstone keeps its row and stalling the watermark behind one is the same under-reporting failure by another route.

`markConversationRead` now uses it in place of `maxSeqForConversation`. `pageBackfill` computes it once per page and clamps BOTH cumulative watermarks with it — `noteDelivered(Math.min(highestInbound, contiguous))` and `noteRead(Math.min(highest, contiguous))` — one extra query per page, on the reconnect path only. Read-on-arrival is clamped for free with the `localMax` the gap check already holds in hand (`m.seq <= localMax + 1 ? m.seq : localMax`, with `localMax === 0` treated as unloaded history rather than a hole), so the inbound hot path pays nothing: the very frame that OPENS a hole now reports read only up to the previous local max instead of claiming everything it skipped.

Covered by `contiguousSeq.test.ts` (6 cases), including both under-reporting traps named above: unloaded history is not a hole, and a tombstone is not a hole.

RESIDUAL, NOT FIXED HERE: the NATIVE ack path this report also named. `PushActionReceiver`'s Mark-as-read and inline-reply branches still POST `/notifications/ack` with the notification's own `seq` unclamped, because that process has no database open to scan — exactly the reason the report called it out. A native Mark-as-read on a conversation with a hole can therefore still over-claim. Worth its own entry if it is judged to matter; the three JS emitters, which are every path that runs with the app alive, are fixed.

testIds: conversationRowIdentity.test.ts: the identity a conversation row shows
chatsList.test.tsx: ConversationRow names a DM whose peer never resolved

bugs.title: A conversation with no resolved name shows as a bare em-dash in the chat list, with no way to tell who it is
bugs.component: apps/mobile/src/features/chat/ui/ChatsList.tsx:140 (and the avatar initial at :82, the accessibility label at :93)
bugs.frequency: Every conversation whose peer name has not been resolved
bugs.reproducibility: Observed live on the real device; deterministic once a row has no name.
bugs.preconditions: A conversation whose peer identity the inbox sync has not resolved and which is not in the address book.
steps: Open the Chats tab.
Look at any row whose peer name has not resolved.
bugs.expected: The row identifies the conversation somehow — the peer's phone number is what WhatsApp shows, or failing that an explicit localised label the user can understand.
bugs.actual: The title renders as a bare em-dash from `{name ?? '—'}`, beside a generic placeholder avatar. The row is completely unidentifiable: the only clue is the message preview. The accessibility label degrades to the literal word 'Chat', so a screen-reader user gets even less, and the avatar initial falls back to '?'.
bugs.user_impact: A conversation in the user's inbox that they cannot identify at all. Observed live with a real row reading '—' and a preview of 'Gd'. Minor in isolation, but it is on the app's home screen and reads as an unfinished state rather than a deliberate one.
bugs.suspected_cause: `{name ?? '—'}` is a placeholder that was never replaced. The row carries `peerId`, but that is an account id and not something to show a user, so the fix needs either the peer's phone number on the row or an explicit localised string — it is not a one-character change, which is presumably why the dash is still there.
bugs.notes:
Found during the live two-device session while checking the chat list; filed after confirming the source. Related to VC-047, which was about the WRONG name being shown; this is about NO name.

FIX: a new pure conversationRowIdentity(name, fallback) in ui/chat/chatModel.ts returns both the title and the avatar initial from ONE decision, so the three places the placeholder used to leak — the visible name, the accessibilityLabel and the avatar initial — can no longer disagree. The label is localised and picked by kind: chat.unknownContact for a DM, chat.unnamedChat for a group, added to all three locales (en, hi, ar) so no locale falls back to English. The avatar is now gated on the initial being absent rather than on a ? sentinel, so an unidentified row draws the same person glyph it always did.

WHY NOT THE PHONE NUMBER, checked in source rather than assumed: the conversations table denormalises peer_id and the avatar but no number; the members endpoint returns bare account ids and the peer profile shape has no phone field at all (contact discovery is OPRF precisely so a number cannot be derived from an account); and the one local number-to-account map cannot reach this case, because the device-contacts reader already falls back to the first NUMBER as the name, so an address-book entry saved without a name arrives with the number AS its name and peerDisplayName returns it. A row that reaches this fallback is by construction one whose peer is not in the address book — nothing on the device holds their number. Resolving one per row would also be a network call on the render path (M0 rule 2) in a list that must recycle at 55+ FPS (R4).

SAME FIX APPLIED TO THE CHAT HEADER in the same pass: an unidentified chat header read "Chats", the bottom-tab label, in the slot where the person name goes. That was the best string available when VC-053 landed; now that chat.unknownContact exists both surfaces say the same thing, and the avatar there is gated the same way. No visual change anywhere — same text slot, font, size, weight, layout and palette.

bugs.title: A notification's Mark-as-read carries the arriving seq, so a late out-of-order push acknowledges below the newest message
bugs.frequency: Whenever FCM delivers two messages for one chat out of order
bugs.reproducibility: Deterministic once the pushes land out of order.
bugs.preconditions: Two messages for the same conversation where the later-sent one is delivered first.
steps: Arrange for push seq 10 to land, then push seq 9 to land after it.
The collapsed notification correctly quotes message 10.
Tap Mark as read.
Check what the sender sees for message 10.
bugs.expected: The action acknowledges the newest message the notification represents — which is what the rebuild after an inline reply already does, reading store.lastSeq.
bugs.actual: Both the Reply and the Mark-as-read PendingIntents were built with showMessage's own `seq` parameter, i.e. the message that happened to arrive last. The notification's PendingIntents carry FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT, so a late push genuinely rewrites the extras to the LOWER seq. Tapping Mark as read then acknowledges up to the late message and dismisses the notification, leaving the newer one unread to its sender until the app is opened.
bugs.user_impact: The user marks a chat read and the sender still sees an unread message. Silent, and only in the out-of-order case the notification-ordering work exists to handle.
bugs.suspected_cause: The actions were built from the arriving message rather than from the per-conversation high-water mark the store already keeps. Fixed by reading store.lastSeq after it has been bumped, exactly as showOwnReply does.
bugs.notes: Found by an adversarial code review of the notification changes made the same day. Same function as the line-ordering fix, whose premise (FCM does not guarantee order) is what makes this reachable.

bugs.title: A notification's collapsed row can show one person's words beside another person's face
bugs.frequency: Group chats where a stored line has no sender id
bugs.reproducibility: Needs a stored line whose sender id was blank.
bugs.preconditions: A group conversation whose notification thread holds a line stored without a sender id.
steps: Receive several messages in a group so the notification thread holds more than one line.
Ensure one stored line has a blank sender id (an older build, or a push with no senderId).
Receive one more message from a DIFFERENT member and look at the collapsed notification.
bugs.expected: The collapsed row's avatar belongs to whoever wrote the text shown beside it.
bugs.actual: `newestSenderId` fell back with `newest?.senderId ?: senderId`, so when the newest line exists but its stored sender id reads back as null, the row showed that line's TEXT with the ARRIVING message's avatar.
bugs.user_impact: In a group, the notification attributes a message to the wrong person at a glance. Small, but it is a misattribution on the lock screen.
bugs.suspected_cause: The elvis guarded the sender id rather than the line. Fixed by guarding on `newest` itself, so the fallback only applies when there is no newest incoming line at all.
bugs.notes: Found by an adversarial code review of the notification changes made the same day.

bugs.title: Mark-as-read and inline reply acknowledge straight over REST from a process with no database, so they can still claim a message the device does not hold
bugs.frequency: Only for a conversation that already has a seq hole
bugs.reproducibility: Needs the hole from VC-051 plus a notification action taken while the app is not running.
bugs.preconditions: A conversation missing a message at some seq, and a notification for a later message in it.
steps: Get the device into the VC-051 state: a message at seq N missing locally while N+1 and above are present.
Receive a later message so a notification appears, with the app not running.
Tap Mark as read (or send an inline Reply) without opening the app.
Look at the tick state for message N on the sender.
bugs.expected: No path acknowledges a seq the device does not hold — the same rule the JS emitters now follow.
bugs.actual: The receiver posts the notification's own seq to POST /notifications/ack directly. Receipts are cumulative, so that covers the missing message. The three JS emitters are clamped to the highest contiguous seq the device holds; this one is not.
bugs.user_impact: The narrow remainder of VC-069: a sender can still be told a message was read when the recipient never received it, but only via a notification action on an already-holed conversation.
bugs.suspected_cause: By design, not oversight — the broadcast receiver runs in a process with no WatermelonDB open, so it cannot compute the contiguous watermark the JS path uses. Closing it needs either a native mirror of the highest safe seq (written by JS whenever it changes) or deferring the ack to the next JS wake, which costs the user the immediate feedback the action exists for.
bugs.notes:
Split out of VC-069 while verifying that fix. Recorded so the VC-069 entry, which reads Fixed, is not taken to cover this path.

FIXED by mirroring the answer instead of trying to compute it where it cannot be computed. The entry itself said the broadcast receiver runs in a process with no WatermelonDB open, so it cannot work out the highest contiguous seq — so javascript, which already computes exactly that for its own receipts (honestWatermark), now pushes it into the native store as safeReadSeq whenever it marks a conversation read. PushActionReceiver clamps its Mark-as-read and Reply acks to min(notificationSeq, safeReadSeq). A conversation native was never told about clamps to nothing rather than to zero, deliberately: a device that has not synced since this build landed must still be able to mark a chat read. The JS binding no-ops on an older native half, so the behaviour there is exactly what shipped before — never worse. NO AUTOMATED TEST: this project has no Kotlin test source set, and the JS half is a one-line mirror; verified by Kotlin compile and code review only.

AUDIT FOUND A HOLE IN THE FIRST VERSION, now closed. The native clamp falls back to the notification own seq when it has never been told a safe watermark (deliberately — a device that has not synced must still be able to mark a chat read), and the watermark was mirrored ONLY from markConversationRead. So a conversation never opened in-app since this build landed was still unclamped, which is the original defect verbatim. The watermark is now mirrored on EVERY inbound message too, using the same clampToHeld the live read path uses, so native policy matches javascript policy instead of approximating it. What remains is only the case javascript itself treats as not-a-hole: a conversation whose first ever message arrives while the app is dead, where the device holds nothing and the skipped range is unloaded history rather than a gap.

bugs.title: Deep links are not gated on a session existing, so a notification could be honoured on a signed-out install
bugs.frequency: Every notification tapped while the app has no session
bugs.preconditions: A notification in the tray and no active session — a sign-out, or any state where the app opens on the sign-in screen while an older notification is still posted.
steps: Have a message notification in the tray.
Get the app into a signed-out state, so it opens on Enter-your-number.
Tap the notification.
bugs.expected: A signed-out app opens at sign-in. A deep link into a conversation must not be honoured without a session.
bugs.actual:
NOT REPRODUCED as originally reported, and the entry is corrected rather than left standing. The report was written from a live observation — the product owner was looking at the Enter-your-number screen, tapped a notification, and landed in a chat. Checked immediately afterwards on the same emulator: three consecutive force-stop + cold starts all landed on the signed-in chat list (confirmed by uiautomator dump, not by eye), so the install HAD a session throughout and the deep link taking it to the chat was correct behaviour, not a bypass. The sign-in screen was a one-off that did not recur; what put it there is still unexplained and is the part actually worth watching.

What IS real, found while checking: the linking config had no session predicate at all. React Navigation resolves an incoming URL against linking.config independently of initialRouteName, so on a genuinely signed-out install the auth gate is not in that path — and notifications outlive a sign-out, because the native side keeps its own credentials to acknowledge a push with no JS alive.
bugs.user_impact: The sign-in gate can be walked around with one tap. Whatever the local database still holds for the previous session is rendered to whoever is holding the phone, and the screen's own effects run against an account that is no longer authenticated.
bugs.suspected_cause: CONFIRMED. `initialRouteName` is chosen from the auth store, but `linking.config` maps `Chat: 'chat/:conversationId'` unconditionally, and React Navigation resolves an incoming URL against that config without consulting the stack's initial route. Notifications outlive a sign-out — the native side keeps its own credentials so it can acknowledge a push with no JS alive — so a stale notification is exactly the trigger.
bugs.notes:
Found by the product owner on a device that had been signed out, during the two-device verification pass. Fixed by giving the linking config a `filter` that reads the auth store when a URL arrives, so a link is only honoured while a session is active.

FIX (defence in depth, not a reproduced-bug fix): linking now carries filter: () => hasSession(). The predicate is deliberately hasSession() — tokens present on the device — and NOT the auth store reporting active. A notification tapped from COLD arrives at the navigation container before the store has hydrated, so asking the store would drop exactly the link this path exists for and land the user on the chat list instead of the chat they tapped, regressing VC-048/VC-053. hasSession reads MMKV synchronously, so it is already true for anyone who has signed in. The first version of this fix did ask the store; it was caught and changed before it shipped.

HONEST STATUS: the gate is correct and cheap, but it closes a hole that was reasoned about rather than observed. The unexplained sign-in screen is NOT explained by it and should be treated as still open if it recurs.

bugs.title: Replying from a notification sends nothing until the app is next opened — the headless service is skipped whenever a React context merely exists
bugs.frequency: Every inline reply taken while the app is backgrounded but its process is still alive
bugs.reproducibility: 100% — this is the ordinary case, because tapping a notification action does not resume the app.
bugs.preconditions: VelChat has been opened at least once since boot (so a React context exists), then backgrounded. A message arrives from the other device and posts a notification.
steps: Device A: open VelChat, then press Home so the app is backgrounded but not killed.
Device B: send a message to Device A.
Device A: pull down the shade, tap Reply on the VelChat notification, type a reply and send it.
Do NOT open the VelChat app.
Watch the notification, and watch Device B for the reply.
bugs.expected: The reply leaves the device immediately and arrives on Device B, with the app never brought to the foreground — that is the entire point of replying from a notification.
bugs.actual: Nothing is sent. The notification sits on 'Sending…' indefinitely and the reply only leaves the device when the user next opens the app, at which point the whole queue drains at once.
bugs.user_impact: The inline reply feature is effectively broken in its normal case: the user believes they have replied, the recipient sees nothing, and the message appears minutes or hours later when the app happens to be opened. Reported live by the user as 'notification se message send nahi ho raha' and 'app open krne pe jata hai message'.
bugs.suspected_cause: queueForJs guarded the fast path with `if (PushBridge.emitPendingEvents(context)) return`. emitPendingEvents answers 'is there a live React context to emit to', not 'will anything act on it'. A backgrounded process still has a context, so the receiver returned early, PushHeadlessService was never started, and javascript — suspended behind the app being in the background — never drained the event. The event sat in the native queue until the next foreground.
bugs.notes:
FIXED in two places.

1. PushActionReceiver.queueForJs now takes the live path only when the app is genuinely RESUMED: `if (PushBridge.isAppResumed(context) && PushBridge.emitPendingEvents(context)) return`. Resumed is the one state where the live path is both faster and certain, because the engine is running and its outbox is not suspended. Everywhere else the headless route is taken, which owns a foreground service for its duration and flushes the outbox before it resolves. Starting it with the process already alive is safe — React Native reuses the instance.

2. The live (resumed) path had the mirror-image gap: it applied the reply to the database but never flushed the outbox, so a reply typed while the app WAS resumed also waited for the next natural flush. pushRuntime's live subscription now awaits syncEngine.flushOutboxNow() after a reply event, matching what the headless path already did.

VERIFIED LIVE, two devices, 2026-09-26: emulator backgrounded (topResumedActivity = launcher throughout), phone sent S1CHECK/S1CHECK2, three inline replies sent from the emulator's notification. logcat shows 'Background started FGS: com.velchat/.push.PushHeadlessService' → 'push: applying queued notification actions' → 'push: handlers done, flushing the outbox' → 'push: outbox flushed' for each, and all three replies ('Hi', 'Kkr', 'Kn') landed on the phone at 10:36 am with the app never foregrounded. No duplicate sends across the three cycles.
